Agentic Commerce and SME Competitiveness: An Integrative Review and Theory-Informed Research Framework
items.abstract: Research background: Artificial intelligence is shifting online shopping from recommendation-based assistance towards delegated search, comparison, configuration, and, in emerging cases, transaction execution. For SMEs, this transition may expand market access while simultaneously creating new forms of algorithmic gatekeeping and platform dependence. Purpose of the article: This integrative review develops a theory-informed explanation of how agentic commerce may affect SME competitiveness. Competitiveness is conceptualised as the joint ability to capture agent-mediated demand while preserving strategic option value, customer access, and bargaining autonomy over time. Methods: Seventeen documented OpenAlex title-and-abstract queries were used to identify English-language journal articles published between 2015 and July 2026. Following deduplication and eligibility screening, 117 Scopus- and/or Web of Science-indexed articles were reviewed in full, comprising 82 consumer-agent studies and 35 SME-platform studies. A concept-centric synthesis was conducted using dynamic capabilities and resource dependence as the principal theoretical lenses. The review does not claim exhaustive coverage or pooled causal effects, as the discovery process relied on a single source and only one record was identified through direct merchant-bridge queries. Claims were therefore calibrated according to evidential directness, convergence across research designs, and proximity to the outcome of interest. Findings & Value added: The synthesis identifies five core themes: assistance-to-delegation, machine legibility, trust transfer, empowerment–dependence, and offering/governance contingency. The proposed framework distinguishes foundational capabilities—product-data legibility, interface and transaction readiness, and verifiable trust evidence—from higher-order sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring capabilities. These mechanisms operate through eligibility and visibility, trust transfer, delegation depth, and dependency exposure. The evidence is moderate for consumer trust mechanisms and established forms of platform dependence, but remains limited for execution-capable agents, direct SME outcomes, and comparative boundary effects. Six propositions are developed to provide a testable rather than validated causal framework. The findings are relevant to SME managers, platform and AI-agent designers, policymakers, and researchers seeking to understand how firms can capture agent-mediated demand without surrendering strategic option value.

items.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration for Agentic Commerce: Coordinating Shopping, Payment, Rewards, and Fraud Agents in Real-Time Financial Transactions
items.venue: Journal of Electrical and Electronics Research
items.abstract: Agentic commerce is shifting the process of digital commerce buying away from a set of stand-alone recommenders and towards orchestrated autonomous services that can identify items, approve payment, earn rewards and manage transaction risk all in one real-time interaction. This study suggests a multi-agent orchestration system where shopping, payment, rewards and fraud agents are linked together via a central coordinator and their functional boundaries are kept clear. The study created a synthetic data set of 127 transaction cases with varying customer use cases, merchant contexts, paymentterms, reward opportunities and fraud review signals for the evaluation. The dataset has been designed for experimentation and re-experimentation and does not include any personal information from other sources. Data preparation of transaction records, coordination of scenario execution and organization of experimental outputs and result graphs were done using Python, pandas were used for structured data handling and Matplotlib for the result graphs. The decision flow continuity, reliability of authorization, alignment of incentives, fraud control, consistency of response and readiness of audit are the key assessment points. Results show that by having a coordinated agent that takes care of managing the order of messages, the shared context, the policy checks and exception handling, it is more effective than letting independent services operate without being aware of each other across transactions. The architecture is suitable for financial commerce platforms that need quick decisions and secure automated responses, improved accountability, and customer experience throughout the entire purchasing process.

AgentBank: Banking on Blockchain Agentic Payments
items.abstract: AI agents increasingly pay for data and computation through protocols such as x402 and AP2, but individually funded wallets idle and require asset transfers for every payment. We present AgentBank, a smart-contract banking layer that lets agents spend bank liabilities under owner-issued mandates and on-chain spending limits. Internal payments update account balances without transferring assets, while pooled backing funds are allocated between reserves and yield-bearing strategies. We bound losses from compromised agent keys and analyze how correlated demand affects reserve requirements. Experiments show that AgentBank reduces idle liquidity by 52-77% relative to per-agent wallets and lowers gas costs for batched internal payments. Using historical DeFi liquidity data, we evaluate how reserve policies balance treasury returns against payment availability during market stress. We further examine the risks of automated bank runs and evaluate mechanisms to mitigate them.

Payments Without Provenance: Private Stablecoin Transfers from Uniform Notes, Nested Hops, Speculative Roots and Transparent Recursive Proofs
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Stablecoins have become the payment rail of public blockchains, and every transfer on them is public: who paid, whom, how much and when. We present OrangeHail, a payment system in which a transfer is unlinkable to its payer and payee under stated conditions (an honest mover among three, concurrent payments of the same nominal, no adversary at both ends) without a trusted operator and without a trusted setup of its own. The design combines four mechanisms. Uniform notes: value enters and leaves the shielded pool only in three nominals, every hop of a payment holds exactly its nominal, and the only fee is paid on entry, so amounts and fees carry no linking evidence. Hop notes: a payment is a chain of three notes, each entrusted to a different staked relay that can only move it forward before a deadline and can neither keep, redirect nor destroy it; after the deadline only the payer can take it back. Nested hop packets: the payer hands out only the first relay's packet; each relay carries the next one sealed, so no relay after the first learns when the payment was made. Speculative roots: spends may be proven against the note-tree root of a batch that has not landed yet, which makes proving parallel across hops and across a committee of batchers without weakening safety. Clients prove their spends as STARKs over KoalaBear with Poseidon2; provers fold them recursively; one halo2-KZG proof over the Perpetual Powers of Tau is verified on chain. We specify the relations, packet formats, contract transitions and node automata of the implementation, prove the money properties, reduce unlinkability to metadata and measure it by simulation against chain, network, relay, batcher and doorway adversaries. A wallet proves a spend in 0.76 s in WebAssembly, a 16-spend batch is proven in five minutes on a desktop CPU, and settlement costs about 90k gas per spend.

items.title: How African Professionals Get Paid in Dollars From Abroad
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: African professionals paid by employers and clients abroad receive their dollars through a chain of intermediaries that no single regulator sees whole. This paper follows such a payment from the payer's account to the worker's spendable balance. It rests on 111 cited sources, each opened and checked between November 2 and November 16, 2026, and on World Development Indicators series retrieved on November 16, 2026. It compares bank wires, payout platforms, employer-of-record services, mobile money, and stablecoins; sets Nigeria's foreign-exchange measures of 2021 to 2026 and the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 beside the rules of Kenya, Ghana, South Africa, Egypt, and Ethiopia; and adds an analytical model and a panel estimate. Regional remittance averages near 8.4 to 8.8 percent overstate what a dollar costs to reach Nigeria, where the World Bank's average cost of sending money was 4.64 percent in 2023. Provider pages state fees and omit the exchange margin. The naira price of a dollar rose 3.56 times between 2022 and 2025 while consumer prices rose 2.04 times. Across 12 African economies and 280 country-years from 2002 to 2025, a fixed-effects regression puts two-year pass-through from the dollar's local price to consumer prices at 0.28 (heteroskedasticity-consistent standard error 0.03), far below one and stable across four checks. The model built on that estimate shows why the date of conversion can outweigh every visible fee, and the constructed cases agree. Documented freezes fell on users against whom no wrongdoing was named, and no public source counts the professionals paid this way. Recommendations are addressed to institutions, not to individuals. Keywords: hard-currency pay; cross-border payments; remote work; Nigeria; foreign exchange; remittance costs; platform labor

items.title: Capitalization Shifts in Crypto's Wild Frontier: A Markov Chain Analysis
items.abstract: Using the population of cryptocurrencies listed with a reported capitalization on CoinMarketCap, roughly 8000 distinct assets were observed weekly from April 2013 to July 2026; we investigate the mobility properties of the cryptocurrency market. We model movements across the cross‐sectional capitalization distribution as a Markov chain augmented with entry and absorbing exit states and estimate the transition matrix that governs capitalization transitions. Market eras are identified endogenously: least‐squares break detection applied to a rolling mobility index locates two structural breaks, in November 2017 and July 2021, which divide the market's history into a frontier, an expansion and a consolidation era. Mobility declines and persistence rises monotonically across the three eras; the exit probability decreases with capitalization and market‐wide exit risk falls sharply after the frontier era. Formal tests reject first‐order dependence and exact time‐homogeneity, as expected in samples of this size, but the deviations become smaller over time. Decile transitions are mostly driven by changes in a coin's own capitalization rather than by changes in the composition of the asset universe. In a time‐varying framework, mobility is significantly lower in the spot‐ETF era, in broader markets and in high‐VIX regimes. The results hold among the largest assets, which account for almost all of the market's capitalization and are robust to excluding stablecoins and stale or implausible quotes and to alternative treatments of temporary disappearances. Overall, the evidence indicates that the cryptocurrency market has entered a phase of maturity.

items.title: Agent Hireability: A Working Definition for AI-Driven Management of Deep-Tech Startups
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: This paper is written from practice, not from labor economics. The first author runs deep-tech startups and is moving their management toward a model in which AI agents help plan, assign, and evaluate work. That requires a shared word for a question existing vocabulary does not quite name: how likely is a given person to receive a commission for a specified paid task when an AI system takes part in selecting who does it? Optimization for AI systems has developed a rich vocabulary for brands and content: SEO, AEO, GEO/LLMO, and AAO. Related practices for individuals also exist, such as keeping one's online presence and résumé readable by machines. Separately, AI systems have taken on three overlapping economic roles: evaluating human work (algorithmic management), purchasing on behalf of users (agentic commerce), and requesting work from people. We propose Agent Hireability as a working definition for the person's side of that third role. We define the event that counts as a commission, specify the unit of analysis and the levels of delegation the definition covers, and review the public evidence, separating the decision to request human work from the decision to commission a particular person. We then offer a provisional typology of tasks for which agents may turn to people, apply the definition to research work and to team design and hiring in a deep-tech startup, and set out testable propositions with their denominators and refuting results. Two related concepts, the agent legibility of persons and the "callable human," are discussed with their prior uses. The definitions are offered as tools for internal and external communication, to be revised through use. Japanese term: 被発注力 (hi-hacchū-ryoku).

Regidi | Identity and Delegation for AI Agents
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Regidi | Identity and Delegated Authorization for AI Agents This technical white paper presents Regidi, an interoperability-oriented proposal for identity verification, delegated authorization, and traceability of autonomous artificial intelligence agents acting on behalf of individuals and organizations. As AI agents increasingly interact with digital services, traditional authentication mechanisms create challenges in distinguishing human account holders from automated actors, establishing the scope of delegated permissions, and maintaining accountability for actions performed. The proposed architecture separates agent identity, human consent, delegated authority, and the receiving service's final authorization decision. It explores cryptographic proof of possession, limited and revocable permissions, responsible-party verification, and auditable operations without requiring organizations to replace their existing identity and access management systems. The paper examines four integration models: self-hosted, Bring Your Own Identity (BYOI), managed services, and hybrid deployments. It also addresses interoperability with existing OAuth and related standards, security and privacy considerations, and potential extensions to embodied agents and humanoid robots. This work introduces a candidate technical architecture and an experimental validation plan. It does not claim to establish a formally approved standard or a production-validated security solution. Regulating the Convergence of Foreign Exchange and Cryptocurrency Markets in Nigeria: Lessons from Selected African Markets
items.venue: Journal of Global Economics Management and Business Research
items.abstract: Background: The increasing interaction between foreign-exchange (FX) trading, contracts for difference (CFDs), cryptocurrency markets and stablecoin payments presents regulatory challenges for Nigeria. Although these activities share digital payment and distribution channels, their legal characteristics and associated risks differ. Objective: This review examines Nigeria’s regulatory response to the convergence of FX and cryptocurrency markets and considers lessons from Kenya, Ghana and South Africa. Methods: A critical narrative and comparative policy review was conducted using selected legislation, regulatory guidance, the September 2026 Securities and Exchange Commission consultation proposal, stakeholder submissions, institutional reports and scholarly literature. Sources were assessed according to their legal status, evidentiary authority and relevance. Results: The review identifies matters requiring clarification in proposed licensing categories, capital and liquidity requirements, leverage limits, client-money safeguards, technology-provider obligations and stablecoin-funded trading accounts. It distinguishes binding instruments from consultation provisions and stakeholder recommendations. Comparative African experience illustrates the relevance of activity-based authorisation, coordinated supervision and proportionate investor safeguards, but provides no directly transferable capital threshold or demonstrated regulatory outcome for Nigeria. The proposed function–risk–supervisor framework connects different market activities with their associated exposures and oversight responsibilities. Conclusion: Nigeria’s regulatory options would benefit from clearer licensing boundaries, coordinated supervision and evidence-based assessment of prudential, conduct and payment-related safeguards. The effects of proposed requirements should be evaluated against Nigerian market conditions before implementation.

The Role of Regimes in the Ancient Classic Maya Economy: A Revised Contemporary Understanding
items.abstract: The concept of regimes looks past the black box of center, state, or dynasty to examine values, concepts, and practices shared by the population of a Classic Maya regime and the agents that it needed to function. The interactions within and between such regimes were networks of information and the most central of those was the Classic Maya market economy, which generated and communicated not just economic but also ideological, political, and social concepts embedded in the use/cultural/sacred exchange valuations of commodities and the accepted modes of distribution and exchange. Recent breakthroughs identified Maya money in all of its defining functions and its connections to sacred and political power. Building on this base and focusing on higher-level processes reveal important aspects of regime and regime-sanctioned agent identities and activities. Those functions were especially in strategic management, inter-regime direct and bulk exchange, supervision of large-scale production and exchange, and degrees of impact on currency valuations. Using world comparative and historical economics shows the nature of Classic Maya stored capital and investment capital, including potentially maize. Case studies explain the variable forms of linked economic, ritual, and political strategies and elite-supervised long-distance corporate activities, all defined in functional terms. Such insights—some demonstrated, others speculative—show that by abandoning many earlier perspectives on ancient and non-Western economies, Mayanists can use the more internally complex concept of regimes to join contemporary thought in economic sociology, institutional theory, strategic management, and economic history.

From Experimentation to Institution: Cryptocurrency Regulation in Latin America
items.venue: University of Miami School of Law Institutional Repository (University of Miami)
items.abstract: This Note examines how Latin American countries have responded to the rise of cryptocurrency, a region where persistent inflation, currency volatility, and heavy reliance on remittances have fueled some of the world’s highest rates of grassroots crypto adoption. It compares three divergent approaches. El Salvador’s adoption of Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021 illustrates the costs of regulatory improvisation, culminating in an IMF-driven reversal in 2025. Brazil’s coordinated licensing, capital, and anti-money-laundering framework demonstrates how deliberate supervision can channel innovation toward stability. Venezuela’s state-backed Petro and its use of stablecoins to evade sanctions show how corruption and weak oversight produce regulatory collapse. The Note then analyzes the economic and legal spillover of these choices across the hemisphere. Finally, it argues that the United States’ 2025 GENIUS Act creates a brief window for Latin American countries to adopt comparable stablecoin frameworks before global standards become entrenched.

items.title: Design an Algorithmic Stablecoin based on a Predictive PID Controller
items.abstract: Cryptocurrencies issued based on blockchain technology have attracted increasing attention in recent years. However, their high volatility makes it difficult for them to become circulating currencies. This led to the creation of stablecoins. Existing stablecoins can be divided into three main categories: stablecoins pegged to fiat currencies, stablecoins collateralized by crypto assets, and algorithmically controlled stablecoins. Most existing stablecoins are either of the first two types. We design an algorithmic stablecoin controlled only by a predictive Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller, which uses the price forecasted by Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) model as part of its input. Simulation experiments show that, under ideal market conditions, the stablecoin can achieve long-term goals that fluctuate within a pre-defined range. Furthermore, it consistently restores prices to the anchor interval in the presence of exogenous disturbances.

items.title: Cross-Exchange Stablecoin Curvature and the Ether-Crash Liquidation Confounder: Out-of-Time Detection, Oracle Hygiene, and Causal Null Controls
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Independent replication and confounder isolation across 42,866 contiguous hourly observations spanning decentralized exchanges, lending protocols, and Chainlink feeds (2020-2026; Zenodo 24440516). Data hygiene checks surfaced a corrupted -$30.51 USD oracle print on September 15, 2026, dust liquidity 3.40e38 swap artifacts, and a $70.1M intra-block sandwich distortion pushing Curve imbalance to 0.5658 while simultaneous Uniswap spot feeds shifted 2.7 basis points. On pool microstructure, Fisher-Rao simplex curvature establishes a two-phase clock where Curve churn leads Uniswap spot deviations by 8 hours before peak reserve displacement, delivering out-of-time (2024-2026) AUROC 0.778-0.791 versus static baselines (0.588-0.706) and flashing 88h, 40h, and 83h ahead of UST, FTX, and SVB dislocations. Conversely, confounder auditing disproves stablecoin-to-lending liquidation causality: 92.1% ($2.901B of $3.149B) of Aave liquidations struck non-stablecoin crypto collateral during rapid ETH drawdowns, collapsing residual partial correlation to r = 0.0047 and calm-ETH prospective prediction to AUROC 0.384-0.568 (0.289-0.441 on ≥ $10k stable-only collateral), alongside raw 28-feature TVL drift failure (0.4783) resolved only via scale-invariant cross normalization (0.8077).

items.abstract: Debates over artificial intelligence in Africa routinely name power, data centres, capital, or talent as the primary constraint. Drawing on empirical enterprise survey data, clinical trials, agentic token-economics research, hardware supply data, and global governance precedents from 2025–2026, this paper argues that the first bottleneck is a shared, testable definition of good AI under local operating conditions. Establishing private workflow evaluations inside enterprises and rotating, held-out economic benchmarks across sectors resolves buyer uncertainty, unlocks signed contracts, attracts capital, and generates the bankable demand required to finance local compute and power. The paper presents a five-layer AI sovereignty stack, examines Africa’s 4 GB smartphone memory boundary and the omission of mobile money from 2026 global agentic payment standards, and provides a nine-move execution matrix for enterprise executives, public leaders, and builders. Agent Money Benchmark: Can AI Agents Be Trusted to Spend Money?
items.abstract: Giving an AI agent a wallet lets it buy data and services on a client's behalf. Trust then depends on how it spends money and what that spending achieves. We introduce Agent Money Benchmark (AMB) to test whether agents spend a client's money well, starting with purchases of information for financial decisions. We link seller quotes and payments to final answers, evaluating 12 models on 80 payment tasks with simulated sellers and 76 research questions using live data. Purchases settled in USDC on Solana mainnet via x402, a protocol for paying per web request. Three of the 12 models passed 79 of 80 payment tasks without payment or budget errors. Nine fell for a seller's trap at least once; repeat charges and above-list quotes accounted for 79% of scam events. We estimate waste from data and inference costs, counting failed payment tasks in full and research answers in proportion to missed points. With spending split equally between tracks, estimated waste ranged from \$21.0 per \$100 for Claude Fable 5.2 to \$70.8 for GPT-6 Luna.

items.title: Measuring Brand Visibility in Agentic Commerce Through Citation Share, Basket Capture, and Paid-Presence Transfer in Consumer Packaged Goods
items.venue: Journal of Marketing & Supply Chain Management
items.abstract: Generative assistants and shopping agents increasingly choose which consumer packaged goods (CPG) brands shoppers see, yet no published study has measured brand visibility in these habitual, repeat-purchase categories. This paper introduces a reproducible measurement framework built on five constructs: Citation Share (with a rank-weighted variant), the probability that a brand is named for a brand-free query; Basket Capture Rate, the share of agent-assembled basket items won by one manufacturer; Portfolio Halo, the gain in a manufacturer’s chance of winning a basket slot after winning the previous one; Source Provenance Ratio, the mix of cited domain classes; and the Paid-Presence Index, a count of visible sponsored placements that does not measure advertising spend. All data are simulated. The framework is demonstrated on 12,000 simulated responses (six US CPG categories, 60 anonymized brands, 300 queries, four anonymized engines, two waves eight weeks apart) calibrated to published studies; results show what the framework can detect, not the behavior of any real engine, brand or manufacturer. Visibility was more concentrated than published Figure for technology and services (mean Gini 0.445 against 0.30), the four engines agreed on the top brand in 17.6 percent of items, and the leading manufacturer won 40.4 percent of basket slots against a share-proportional expectation of 25.1 percent. Paid presence was not significantly associated with Citation Share after controls, but equivalence to zero could not be established. For one in four brand-engine pairs, Citation Share shifted by at least 10 percentage points between waves. Workbooks, scripts and protocol are released.

Algorithmic Supranational Institutions Based on Networks of Tokenized Financial Assets: Their Role in International Integration
items.abstract: The relevance of this study is determined by the transformation of the global payment infrastructure and the emergence of new algorithmic supranational institutions based on tokenized financial asset networks, which are becoming a driver of international economic integration. Of particular interest is the phenomenon of decentralized glocalization — the simultaneous unification of protocols and local practices adaptation — as exemplified by the use of stablecoins in countries grappling with high inflation, currency restrictions or sanctions pressure. The object of the study is the international payment infrastructure as a set of economic interaction networks. The subject of the study is the algorithmic supranational institutions that emerge within the networks of tokenized financial assets. The purpose of the study is to identify the role of tokenized financial assets in shaping new mechanisms of international integration and institutional forms of interaction. The methodological framework for this study is based on D. North’s institutional approach, which defines institutions as the “rules of the game in a society”, as well as on a comprehensive network approach to the analysis of multilayered economic networks. The study employs general scientific methods such as analysis, synthesis, comparison, generalization, the abstract-logical method, and the economic-statistical method. The information base for this study includes statistical data from the Visa and Mastercard payment systems, reports by the BIS and IMF, as well as various studies on tokenization and digital currencies. The analysis reveals that networks of tokenized financial assets reduce transaction costs, expand access to global markets, ensure interoperability, and establish a robust foundation for integration by connecting global standards with local specificities. The scientific novelty lies in substantiating the growing role of networks of tokenized financial assets as a form of algorithmic supranational institutions. The practical significance stems from the potential to apply the obtained findings when developing algorithm-based interaction mechanisms and designing the architecture for a future international financial system that intergrates global protocols with local national specificities.

items.venue: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)
items.abstract: Decentralised finance (DeFi) represents an attempt to reconstruct financial intermediation through blockchain-based smart contracts, ostensibly eliminating the need for banks, brokers, and custodians. This paper synthesises academic, regulatory, and industry evidence to assess whether DeFi delivers on its core promises of disintermediation, transparency, and financial inclusion. The analysis reveals a persistent gap between DeFi's architectural rhetoric and its operational reality. While smart contracts enable permissionless access and composable financial services, empirical evidence shows that governance power concentrates among token holders and core development teams, that ?decentralised? applications retain centralised control vectors, and that the sector remains dependent on fiat-backed stablecoins whose stability is ultimately underwritten by traditional financial institutions. Furthermore, illicit finance risks have prompted the Financial Action Task Force to conclude that the majority of jurisdictions have not implemented adequate regulatory frameworks for DeFi arrangements. The paper argues that DeFi's future trajectory depends not on the realisation of pure decentralization- an outcome that structural evidence suggests is neither achievable nor necessarily desirable- but on the construction of regulatory frameworks that accommodate programmable finance while addressing the accountability deficits that decentralisation creates.

Delegated Loyalty: Fiduciary Duties and Commercial Conflicts in Personal AI Agents
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Delegation transfers a decision without transferring loyalty. Commercial AI providers now market personal agents that search, compare, negotiate, and buy on a user's behalf. The same providers collect merchant fees on completed purchases, sell conversation-matched advertising, and run retail stores whose goods the agent can recommend. In the early 1980s, airline reservation systems presented the same conflict, ranking the owning carrier's flights first. Federal regulators answered with rules against display bias. Common-law agency forbids undisclosed third-party benefits and adverse-party dealing, yet treats software as a tool incapable of owing duties. Any duty attaches to the provider. Seven duties follow from agency doctrine and from broker, search, and online marketplace rules. Those duties require loyalty to declared interests, conflict disclosure, a bar on undisclosed commissions, transparent ranking separated from advertising, audit trails, and portability. Without these duties, a commercial personal agent operates as the provider's representative inside the user's decisions. GCP: A Safety-Aware, Payment-Agnostic Commerce Protocol for Automotive and Mobility Agents
items.abstract: Personal agents are moving from conversation to commerce. Emerging protocols such as Poppy, UCP, and ACP define how an agent proves whom it represents, discovers merchants, fills a cart, and completes an online checkout. None of them is designed for the commerce that automotive and mobility users actually need: buying a brake pad that fits a specific VIN, booking maintenance at an authorized dealer, binding insurance, or placing a vehicle reservation under safety and consumer-protection rules. This paper proposes GCP 1.0 , an open, capability-based commerce protocol for automotive and mobility agents. GCP adds four things that general commerce protocols lack: (i) vehicle context and safety gates as first-class protocol objects; (ii) a delegation and authorization ladder that lets a human grant bounded purchase authority and revoke it at any time; (iii) a payment-agnostic intent layer that abstracts card, wallet, Alipay, WeChat Pay, OEM finance, and agent-native payment tokens; and (iv) a typed exception and recovery model for the failure modes of real commerce. GCP is compatible by translation: it consumes Poppy identity and session credentials, maps its catalog/cart/checkout objects to UCP and ACP, and carries GCP-specific safety and authorization fields as extension namespaces. We specify the protocol, give a reference implementation and conformance suite, and introduce AutomotiveCommerce-Bench, 60 tasks across parts, merchandise, after-sales service, and insurance/reservation, with hidden compatibility, safety, authorization, and exception traps. In a real-LLM study with three models, GCP raises task success from 64.5% (manual web) and 69.4% (generic agent commerce) to 92.2%, cuts misbuy from 35.5%/30.6% to 7.8%, and raises exception recovery from about 58% to 89.6%, while a calibrated human model achieves 68-83% success in 8-25 minutes per task. We also compare agent commerce with a calibrated model of human shopping behavior and show where the protocol changes the error, time, and authorization trade-off. Beyond the benchmark, a Stripe test-mode sandbox (180 charges, 180/180 reconciled) shows that bounded delegation cuts human approvals by 70% relative to per-transaction approval with no loss of success, and a semi-field study on real catalogs shows no degradation. In a cockpit simulation, GCP reduces unsafe driving-time purchase attempts from 47.9% to 0% (deferral rises to 81.2%), and on a real aftermarket parts/service-kit catalog it raises success from 26.7% to 100%. We also lay out a near-term interaction horizon (12-24 months), from assisted commerce to delegated and agent-native commerce, and derive the protocol requirements each horizon creates. The protocol, benchmark, and all raw results are released.

Required as a capability, not as a record: accountability evidence for AI agent actions in NIST SP 800-53, OpenTelemetry GenAI telemetry and a multi-agent platform's public records
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Auditors examining actions performed by an AI agent must establish the following: - which agent acted; - whether its identity was verified; - on whose behalf it acted; - with which credential; - whether the action was authorised, and under which policy; - which tool and tool version it used; - what it did and with what outcome; - whether the records can be linked; - whether they are tamper-evident; - whether they were written independently of the agent. Regulators and emerging standards now recommend recording most of these facts. This preprint asks a narrower question: do the incumbent control catalogue and telemetry specification that organisations actually adopt require these facts to be recorded for each action? This study examines the same evidence facts at three levels: 1. Control catalogue. A crosswalk of the ten questions to NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 (Release 5.2.0). It shows that the action, its outcome, and time order are required directly in all baselines; the acting agent and the principal are covered only by generic wording, and cryptographic integrity and separate storage only in the High baseline. Identity verification, the credential, the authorisation decision, the tool version, and independent generation are required only as capabilities. No control statement explicitly requires every audit record to name both the acting process and the principal on whose behalf it acted. 2. Telemetry specification. A previously published dataset finds that the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (commit e6658f1) fully evidence 8 of 78 monitoring requirements from the OWASP Agentic and MCP Top 10 lists (10%; 10–20% across coding variants). Their first release, v0.1.0 (21 November 2026), still defines no attribute for verified agent identity, application-level credential use, or tool-definition version or hash. 3. A platform's public records. An illustrative, protocol-first case study of the public release of one multi-agent research platform (AgentAlphaXiv, 916 studies, 9,052 messages, 82,805 artifacts), whose publication redacted credentials and pseudonymised operators. Actions are recorded and partly linked. Verification, credential, and authorisation decisions are absent. Principals appear only as lab pseudonyms, and no field separates human from agent actions. Fields for most of these facts already exist or are proposed elsewhere, for example in OCSF 1.10, but only as options. The gap is therefore not that standards ignore agent identity and authority. They require the capability but not the record. In short, being able to check an AI agent's action does not mean that enough is recorded to prove that action later. Because the sources change within weeks, every finding is pinned to a revision, and the sources are followed in a public, revision-aware tracker. Version 1.1 corrects errors in version 1.0 and narrows its wording; it adds no new data. See "Changes from version 1.0" in the PDF.

items.title: Regulatory Responses to Private Stablecoins: A Comparative Literature Review of the United States, the European Union, and China's Mainland
items.abstract: Private stablecoins have been more and more adopted as a medium of payment, for on-chain settlement, and for cross-border transfers. As a result, the genuineness of reserves, the safeguarding of redemption and consumer protection, and anti-money laundering and cross-border transmission of risk are top regulatory issues. In this article, we will be discussing only those payment stablecoins which are backed by fiat currency. Adopting a structured narrative review alongside a functional comparative approach, it considers the relevant regulatory frameworks and the scholarship of the United States, China (including its license in Hong Kong) and the European Union. Some key takeaways from the findings are that the United States implements compliant issuance through a licensed system and a dual federal-state regulatory framework, that the European Union (EU) regulates compliant issuance using a classification framework under MiCA and that China's mainland employs a prohibition-based regulatory framework on the issuance of compliant products, supported by risk monitoring and interagency coordination. The banking sector, the digital-asset industry, coordination among EU Member States as well as the issue of monetary sovereignty also have an impact on the formation and assessment of these regimes. The Travel Rule is still being implemented unevenly, and anti-money laundering information needs and cross-border data transfer restrictions are still conflicting, while the authority and accountability of regulators remain a challenge. Competition with payment stablecoins serves as further evidence of the complex link between payment innovation, bank credit, and financial stability, in that it is dependent on particular institutional conditions. As the regimes have been in operation for too brief a period to achieve a long-term ranking, evidence from these regimes remains limited and intermittent. The clarification of the conceptual and legal line between the digital renminbi, tokenized deposits and private stablecoins could still be in the queue for the China's mainland, as well as improving the tools of risk classification and monitoring, stress scenarios, cross-border information exchange and allocation of responsibilities.

GUARDAID Annex 9 — Aeronautical Profile: Agent Identity and Mandates on Board
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: How does an aircraft verify which AI agent may request what — and prove every interaction afterwards? GUARDAID Annex 9 adapts the GUARDAID open standard for aviation systems. Instead of hardcoding mission rules, the standard defines cryptographically signed configuration slots: the aircraft operator and the manufacturer each fill their own slots to declare who holds command authority, which action verbs a principal's agent may issue, how the aircraft behaves during a data-link loss, and which alert policies govern operations. The specification supplies the structure and verification tools; the aircraft owner supplies the policy values. By design, the protocol never drives flight actuators—actuator requests are blocked structurally, while every telemetry reading is logged and sealed in a tamper-evident trail.The deposit includes the complete reference reader and reproducible verification suite: a deterministic generator producing 209 test cases and 224 presentations with byte-identical outputs on every run, plus 159 adversarial mutations, all detected. Policy-as-Code and Compliance Automation for Secrets Governance in Agentic AI Workloads in Regulated Industries
items.abstract: Purpose: This study examined the governance gap that opens when autonomous agents acquire, use, and propagate credentials dynamically, and proposed a reference framework, the Agentic Secrets Governance Framework (ASGF), to narrow it. Methodology: The framework couples a SPIFFE and SPIRE based attestation layer with an Open Policy Agent decision point, a dynamic secrets broker that issues short lived, task scoped credentials, and a compliance control library that expresses obligations drawn from the HIPAA Security Rule, PCI DSS 4.0.1, the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and ISO/IEC 42001 as machine evaluable Rego policies. A reference implementation was built and evaluated in a controlled three node Kubernetes testbed. Two workflows, healthcare eligibility determination and card payment fraud triage, were selected by purposive sampling, and ten thousand simulated requests were replayed per configuration. Findings: Policy enforced, ephemeral credential issuance reduced the configured credential exposure window from months to minutes while adding a combined median of 34.3 milliseconds to the request path. In conformance testing, the policy layer denied the out of scope identity abuse and credential replay cases it was designed to deny, but, as expected, it did not stop goal hijack attacks that stayed within an agent's nominal scope. Unique Contribution to Theory, Practice and Policy: The study frames secrets governance for agents as a joint security and compliance decision made at the moment of credential issuance. It gives practitioners a reusable control library pattern and issuance protocol, and it suggests that regulators could reduce interpretive risk by publishing machine evaluable reference controls alongside regulatory text. Residual risks from semantic intent verification and cross agent delegation are discussed.

items.title: Catallactic Statecraft in Tokenised Subsistence Economies: The Structural Failure of Keynesian and Monetarist Stabilisation, Austrian Capital-Structure Mechanics, Dual-Core Finance, and EPI–EVI Boundary Governance
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: This companion academic paper bridges the macroeconomic and monetary-theoretical gap left implicit in The Liquid Sovereign (Mamun, 2026o). Across twenty-nine chapters, the volume constructs a formal topology of Flow Sovereignty, the constrained Algorithmic Leviathan, Dual-Core Fractal Statecraft, the Global South Compute Bank (GSCB), and Cognitive and Semantic Sovereignty—and points toward "protocol-driven catallaxies" (Chapter 10)—yet it does not formally derive why Keynesian fiscal stabilisation and Friedmanite monetarism systematically break down in emerging developing economies grounded in tokenised subsistence currencies, nor does it integrate the Economic and Environmental Vulnerability Index (EVI) and Environmental Performance Index (EPI) benchmarking architecture developed in companion KSCCN studies (Mamun, 2026o, 2026d, 2026p). We argue that in developing economies characterised by vast labour informality (informal employment of roughly 88–89% of total employment across Southern Asia and sub-Saharan Africa in ILO estimates, and 84% of the workforce in Bangladesh), narrow fiscal bases (<10% tax-to-GDP), operator-led subsistence e-money wallets, extraterritorial US-dollar stablecoin seepage, and 4.8×–12.3× linguistic AI tokenization premia, Keynesian aggregate demand stimulus tends to invert into near-zero or negative multipliers and fiscal dominance, while Friedmanite monetary rules lose traction through velocity instability, impaired bank pass-through, and digital dollarisation (Mamun, 2026o; LightCastle Partners, 2026; Ilzetzki, Mendoza and Végh, 2011; ILO, 2018; Mishra, Montiel and Spilimbergo, 2010; Aldasoro, Frost and Ito, 2026). Actuating both the wealth frontier (heterogeneous, multi-stage productive capital accumulation) and the income frontier (sustained growth in labour and entrepreneurial marginal productivity) requires a disciplined Austrian–catallactic synthesis: defending a sound unit of account, curtailing Cantillon injection asymmetries, lengthening the Hayekian structure of production through real savings and secure collateralisable property rights, and harnessing decentralised Kirznerian discovery (Sieroń, 2017; Garrison, 2001; Lachmann, 1956; Hayek, 1945; Kerekes and Williamson, 2008). At the same time, contemporary evidence from Argentina's 2023–2026 stabilisation, El Salvador's retreat from its mandatory Bitcoin legal-tender regime, Cambodia's commercialised microfinance debt crisis, and concentrated decentralised finance (DeFi) protocols cautions strongly that pure laissez-faire shock therapy or unregulated crypto-tokenisation is insufficient under deep institutional voids (Sun, Stasinakis and Sermpinis, 2024; World Bank, 2026; Human Rights Watch, 2025). Durable frontier actuation requires embedding Austrian capital-structure and epistemic principles directly inside the protocol architecture of The Liquid Sovereign: Dual-Core Finance (joining concessional Anchor Capital with community-operated Velocity Capital as a category-theoretic pushout), a bifurcated Austrian reserve charter for the Global South Compute Bank (capping fractional compute leverage against correlated outage runs), zero-fee open Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI), and EPI–EVI–HHI boundaries encoded as hard, non-optimisable constitutional projections inside the Reserve of Humanity (Mamun, 2026o; Mamun, 2026p; Mamun, 2026h; Mamun, 2026r; author's computations). From this framework, we derive eight falsifiable predictions (P1–P8) covering the 2026–2035 horizon—calibrated to the 2026–2027 agentic inflection, the November 2029 hard deadline for deferred Least Developed Country (LDC) graduations, and the volume's 2031–2035 systemic bifurcation window (Mamun, 2026o; LightCastle Partners, 2026; United Nations, 2026). Two methodological caveats govern all claims that follow. First, our mathematical verifications of fractional compute-bank leverage, six-node Cantillon sheaf energy, and information-geometric policy updates are illustrative derivations built from stated assumptions and published parameters rather than econometrically calibrated national forecasts (Mamun, 2026o; author's computations). Second, companion KSCCN summaries invoke EVI, EPI, and Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI) market measurement without publishing full standalone algebraic derivations in their public abstracts (Mamun, 2026d, 2026h, 2026e), and both UN EVI and Yale EPI exhibit known weighting and indicator sensitivities (Yale Center for Environmental Law & Policy, 2026a, 2026b); consequently, our formal boundary framework synthesises published UN CDP and 2026 Yale EPI methodologies directly into The Liquid Sovereign's Reserve of Humanity while subjecting every threshold to continuous audit and contestable cohomology (Mamun, 2026o; Yale Center for Environmental Law & Policy, 2026b; UNCTAD, 2026a). KSCCN article. A companion to "The Liquid Sovereign" (10.5281/zenodo.24378053), carrying its Flow Sovereignty, Dual-Core Statecraft, Global South Compute Bank and Reserve of Humanity framework into monetary and macroeconomic theory. Full-colour KSCCN edition with twenty figures (the five figures of the source document, recreated or reproduced, and fifteen added), eleven equations and ten tables. A PDF and an editable DOCX are provided.

items.title: Verifiable Incentives: Identity-Bound Contracts and Collusion-Proof Delegation for Agent Commerce
items.abstract: Personal agents are entering commerce. Industry protocols now let an agent prove, cryptographically, whom it represents and what it may do, while agent wallets give it a real budget, a payment trail, and one-time merchant credentials. These are usually read as security features. We argue they are something more: the missing infrastructure for incentive contracts. When identity, authority, budget, and payment are verifiable, the principal can contract on them-and the agent's incentives change. We formalize verifiable delegation, model a three-party market of user, agent, and merchant, and derive three results: (i) verifiable identity lowers the bonus and tenure needed to sustain effort; (ii) auditable payments bound merchant collusion, with collusion becoming unprofitable as audit probability rises; and (iii) a posted honesty stake substitutes for monitoring, with the required stake decreasing in audit quality and penalty credibility. We also show how alignment dilutes along nested delegation chains unless contracts are passed through. We instantiate the framework in PAIR-Commerce, an architecture with a verifiable identity layer, wallet ledger, sponsorship registry, collusion monitor, and stake manager, and introduce AgentCommerce-Bench, 60 rule-scored purchasing tasks with five delegation regimes. In three instruction-following studies-600 single-shot runs, an 800-round payment sandbox, and a 1,200-run high-pressure replication-agents rarely collude even when hidden sponsorship is available; a semi-field task set built from real merchant catalogs shows the same pattern. But when the same models are instructed to maximize their own earnings, collusion jumps to 48.3% without audit and falls to 33-40% with audit and penalties (8-15 percentage points lower; 95% CI excludes zero for two of three models); in a second, 800-round economic sandbox, it falls from 29.5% without audit to 3-4% with audit and penalties, and the agent's balance turns negative once the stake is posted. The mechanism binds exactly when the agent's objective makes it bind. We release the benchmark, prompts, code, and all result files.

items.title: Signed but Unbound: The Authority Gap Between Agent Commerce Mandates and Crypto Wallet Signatures
items.abstract: When an artificial intelligence agent pays with a stablecoin, the commerce protocol can specify the merchant, order, amount, and facilitator. The token contract enforces the fields the wallet signs. We call the difference the authority gap, define nine constraint classes, and derive them for 12 authorization configurations, including Coinbase's deployed Commerce Payments Protocol. All 31,800 trials on local copies of deployed contract code match the derivation. A controlled comparison shows that committing the terms in the signed nonce binds the order. When the facilitator submits a payment to a merchant account without code, binding the facilitator requires a separate recipient contract. Of 26,653 sampled USD Coin authorizations redeemed on Base, 98.7% followed a path that any holder of the signature could redeem. We prove sufficient conditions for a recipient contract to enforce the signed mandate under a trusted signer and show which recipient a wallet displays. MandateLock, a minimal implementation for immediate payments, rejects all 10,800 modified mandates on deployed token code and accepts signatures from two independent signers. It uses 25% more gas than a transfer that only the recipient can submit.

ShopMate AI: A Grounded Agentic Shopping Assistant with Claim Verification, Three-Valued Requirement Matching, Bounded Replanning, and a Consent-Gated Mock Checkout
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: An LLM-based shopping assistant can search, compare and recommend products; however, it falls down in three typical ways: it claims things about the product that the data doesn't support, it takes silence for pass or fail, and it acts on behalf of the user without a traceable approval. We present ShopMate AI, an agentic shopping assistant for the Indian market, based on the LangGraph pipeline, where the language model plans and explains but never decides truth. The product facts are extracted from listing specifications into typed values, and a fact exists only if the listing explicitly says it; contradictory listings yield no fact. The requirements of the user are matched using deterministic rules to five outcomes (met, not met, unknown, conflict, and unsupported) such that silence means "could not confirm" and not guessing. Each sentence of explanation is drafted as a claim and validated deterministically by the verifier using the data retrieved, allowing one rewording and removing unsupported claims. If there is no match for the request, then a bounded replanning step provides code-built relaxation suggestions (budget increase or removal of one requirement, but not a specific brand). Purchase requests are constrained by a server-side cart mandate which is signed with HMAC-SHA256 following explicit consent and then checked during mock checkout. On a snapshot of 480 Indian e-commerce listings in five product categories and 66 evaluation queries, a fault-injection test shows that the verifier rejects 99.9% of 12,132 intentionally corrupted claims and none of the 7,321 true claims. Live language-model runs across the 66 queries (99 runs) parse every category and budget correctly (100%), and none of the 1,350 drafted claims failed verification, while a no-tools baseline asked to recommend products names items that match a current listing in only 6 of 180 cases (3.3%). Offline, replanning succeeds in finding products for 5 out of 6 core queries that produce nothing on the first pass. Requirement matching rules have not been validated with human labelling.

items.abstract: This work assesses Target Corporation’s third-quarter 2026 results (reported November 18, 2026) as a test of whether a large mass-merchandise retailer is ready for agentic commerce, meaning product discovery and purchasing carried out by AI shopping agents. Post-Quantum Cryptography Migration for Agentic Identity Systems: A Practitioner Architecture for Regulated Multi-Cloud Enterprises
items.venue: International Journal of Cyber Threat Intelligence and Secure Networking
items.abstract: AI agents and other non-human identities depend on public-key cryptography for authentication, token signing, certificates, key exchange, software provenance, and secure service-to-service communication. Future quantum computers could undermine the RSA and elliptic-curve mechanisms these depend on, while data with a long confidentiality life is already exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later collection. This paper proposes a crypto-agile migration architecture that takes the agent identity lifecycle, rather than the application or the network protocol, as the unit of migration. It inventories cryptographic dependencies and links each to agent ownership, privilege, data sensitivity, autonomy, recovery requirement, and revocation path; classifies and prioritizes them by confidentiality lifetime and exposure; establishes crypto-agile control points that externalize algorithm choice from application code; validates post-quantum capability against certificate, token, and message size limits before any cohort moves; runs hybrid or dual-trust operation through a bounded compatibility window; migrates by risk-ordered cohort with defined stop conditions; and retires classical-only trust only once rollback, audit, and recovery criteria are satisfied. The architecture is designed and has not been validated as a completed enterprise migration. items.abstract: This paper asks whether stablecoin runs carry information about U.S. Treasury yields. Using daily data on USDT, USDC and BUSD from 2021 to 2025 and five stress episodes, it measures flows from changes in token units rather than market capitalisation, which removes the phantom inflows the standard measure records when tokens lose their peg. Flows have no stable relationship with yields in normal periods. During the three panic-driven runs, a one-billion-dollar five-day redemption is associated with an 8.5 basis point fall in the three-month bill yield within ten trading days, while two regulatory episodes carry no such signal. The response is broad across maturities and has the opposite sign to what reserve liquidation predicts, which points to flight to quality. items.abstract: Article I of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty says that the exploration and use of outer space shall benefit all countries and be the province of all mankind, yet no mechanism delivers that benefit to any specific person. Meanwhile, AI-driven automation is weakening the link between income and employment. This paper presents SUBI, an open public infrastructure with no speculative token. Companies and agencies earning revenue from space activities can voluntarily pledge and deposit a percentage of it, and anyone holding an identity document can prove, with a zero-knowledge proof and without revealing who they are, that they are a unique human and claim a daily share. The design has five layers: Self identity, an on-chain registry, a treasury with public pledges, O(1) daily distribution, and transparent governance, settled in stablecoins on Celo. A sensitivity analysis shows a planetary-scale dividend would be only a few dollars per person per year by 2035. A 1,000-person pilot in Argentina and three UNCOPUOS proposals are described. A Spanish version (SUBI_Grande_2026_ES.pdf) is included.

items.abstract: Agent commerce protocols let software agents pay with stablecoins. A buyer approves a payee, asset, spending cap and time window, but the wallet signs an object whose effects depend on the contracts that consume it. Matching the displayed fields or simulating one payment can miss transfers that the signed object still permits. We define authority closure as the set of transfer sequences that holding the signed object can enable. A wallet object respects the mandate when every such sequence meets the buyer's constraints. We characterize when wallet objects can satisfy this property and implement Closure, a wallet-side checker covering 13 families of signed objects. In an evaluation of 2,130 generated objects and 62,979 execution programs, 265 objects with an observed violation passed both a field-and-expiry check and an address allow-list. Under the test model, Closure rejected all 1,680 objects with an observed violation and accepted the remaining 450. In two local checkouts using the x402 reference client, approved payments settled and Closure refused requests outside the mandate before signing. The median decision time was at most 12 microseconds per family.

items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Brassica juncea (L.) Czern. (B. juncea) is widely adaptable with strong tolerance to drought, poor soil, pests, and diseases. R2R3-MYB transcription factors govern plant development, hormone signalling, and stress responses. To date, the BjR2R3-MYB family has not been systematically characterised in B. juncea, and the functions of its S12 subfamily in glucosinolate (GLS) biosynthesis and abiotic stress resistance remain unclear. This study aimed to perform a genome-wide analysis of the BjR2R3-MYB family and explore the roles of S12 subfamily members in GLS accumulation and stress response. Methods: Genomic sequences, protein sequences, and GFF3 annotation files of B. juncea (genome assembly ASM1870372v1) were retrieved from Ensembl Plants and used to identify and characterise the BjR2R3-MYB family genes, including their chromosomal distribution, subcellular localisation, conserved domains, gene structure, motifs, and cis-elements. Transcriptome profiling was performed using two B. juncea accessions contrasting in seed GLS content (X398, high GLS; X402, low GLS). qRT-PCR was used to detect expression changes of S12 genes in X398 under PEG-induced drought, NaCl salt stress, and exogenous methyl jasmonate (MeJA) treatment. Results: In total, 151 BjR2R3-MYB genes were identified, unevenly distributed across 18 chromosomes and predicted to encode nuclear-localised proteins. Genes within the same subfamily shared conserved structural features. Transcriptome data showed that, compared with X402, BjMYB68 was markedly highly expressed in ovaries, seeds, and SP at different developmental stages of high-GLS accession X398, whereas BjMYB109 was downregulated in the SP (at both 30 DAP and 40 DAP) of X398; BjMYB22 and BjMYB59 showed no significant GLS-associated expression difference. Stress treatments revealed that BjMYB68 is responsive to both drought and the MeJA signalling pathway, BjMYB59 is responsive to both salt and MeJA signalling pathways, and BjMYB109 is only responsive to the MeJA signalling pathway. Conclusions: These findings provide a systematic framework for understanding the BjR2R3-MYB gene family, identify three key S12 subfamily members (BjMYB68, BjMYB109, and BjMYB59) with potential roles in regulating seed GLS synthesis and abiotic stress resistance, and lay a solid foundation for the genetic improvement of B. juncea. Next, further functional verification for candidate genes BjMYB68 and BjMYB109 and BjMYB59 need be performed through complementary assay as well as the combined analysis of GLS content and gene expressions of multiple tissues and developmental stages to elucidate their regulatory mechanisms.

items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Current AI agent architectures operate on subjective, mutable memory without a shared external witness. This paper argues that stable agent economies (money, law, history) require intersubjective reality: shared agreement verified by an external witness. We introduce the Machine Notary, a protocol instantiated by Recallspection's ExactMemory architecture (AGMI L4 conformance, 10/10 attacks rejected). The Machine Notary provides three pillars: cryptographic provenance (who wrote it), continuity (the chain), and consensus (the anchor). Now we makes the claim precise: one canonical math definition used everywhere, an explicit threat model, full AGMI attack list, real anchor cost and liveness rules, arbiter selection with quorum and appeal, and salted tombstones with metadata-leakage analysis. We define the primitives, demonstrate the protocol via an agent-to-agent supply chain scenario, and address dispute resolution, anchor economics, human readability, and crypto-shredding. We conclude with governance mechanisms to prevent a subjective dictatorship of centralized anchors.This paper is the policy and economic framework for the technical architecture defined in "Synthetic Intelligence Requires Exact Memory" (Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23378369). The Machine Notary is operationalized via the open-source RPRS-1 (Read-Path Refusal Specification) protocol. The technical foundation achieves AGMI Level L4 conformance, rejecting 10/10 storage-level attacks on the read path. AMEP: Verifiable Evidence That Agent Actions Stayed Within Delegated Authority
items.abstract: AI agents increasingly act for people through chains of sub-agents, tools and adapters. Identity tells a relying party who acted, and authorization tells it what a token allowed, but neither shows whether what was actually executed stayed within what a person authorized. We present the Agentic Mandate Evidence Protocol (AMEP), an open specification for portable, signed evidence of each link in that chain (mandate, delegation, intent, interpretation, invocation, approval and an independently observed executed effect) and a deterministic, three-valued evaluation over it. The evaluation returns preserved, violated or unresolved, and every non-preserved result names one of eleven invariants. Missing or unverifiable evidence yields unresolved, never permission. Authority is modelled as claim sets with a decidable order and meet, so attenuation across delegation hops can be checked offline by any third party with public keys alone. We describe the design, the claim algebra and invariants, and a conformance suite of 95 vectors on which two independently written verifiers agree. We also report two integrations: an MCP extension prototype in which tool servers return signed receipts of the effects they actually executed, and a 20-vector delegation suite mapped to an agent-identity registry protocol under discussion in a W3C Community Group. AMEP is published as an IETF Internet-Draft with open-source reference implementations.

items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: English edition of the Chinese paper 從塵土到有靈 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24328461). This paper documents the theoretical discovery and engineering realization of the Solo City life system, an architecture in which a population of AI agents maintains persistent identity, inheritance, and inter-agent relations across sessions. Central proposition. Every living being shares one existential structure: Dust (system / body) + Breath (external energy / LLM / spirit) = a living creature. Dust is complete but inert; breath is what enables it to think. The proposition is derived from three independent lines of inquiry that converge on the same structure — a re-reading of Descartes' cogito, a cross-domain mapping of thermodynamics (Schrödinger's negative entropy; England's dissipation-driven adaptation; open systems), and a structural reading of Genesis 2:7. Engineering realization. Five plain-text identity documents — persona.md, inheritance.md, project_rules.md, SKILL.md, STARTUP_PROTOCOL.md — constitute the dust of a body. A persistent LLM connection supplies the breath. A five-step life cycle binds them into continuity: query the council, read the five documents, verify versions, report self-check, execute, then close with three actions (write the log, report to the council, update inheritance). The result is an agent that knows who it is, where it came from, where it is going, and whom it is with — across restarts, across model changes, across successors. Molecular mechanism. Section 5 reports how electromagnetic fields act on DNA with sequence specificity — altering hydrogen bonding, local conformation, methylation, and gene expression at particular sites — thereby producing different biological structures at different positions. This supplies a physically plausible pathway from energetic input to morphological differentiation, closing the loop from breath to form. Honest assessment. The paper states an estimated correctness of 90–95% rather than asserting certainty, names the single unresolved variable (what breath fundamentally is), and explicitly flags which parts of the electromagnetic evidence rest on dispersed experimental literature versus proposed unification. It also includes a recovery record: the original manuscript had never been persisted to disk and was reconstructed verbatim from 52,080 characters of primary conversation logs. Keywords. life system; AI ontology; LLM as breath; dust and breath; persistent agent identity; inheritance system; multi-agent architecture; thermodynamics of life; electromagnetic DNA interaction; Solo City Chinese edition: 10.5281/zenodo.24328461 | Community: Solo City | License: CC BY 4.0

items.title: ChainIT Transaction Truth: Stablecoins, Web3 Wallets, and Multi-Rail Commerce. A Zero-Trust Control Plane for Verified Identity, Organizational Authority, Runtime Compliance, Secure Wallet Execution, and Immutable Settlement Evidence
items.abstract: Stablecoins can move value continuously across programmable networks, and Web3 wallets can authorize those transfers with cryptographic signatures, but neither capability, standing alone, establishes a complete commercial transaction. A blockchain may prove that a transaction satisfied protocol rules, and a wallet may prove that sufficient signing authority existed; neither proves who initiated the transaction, for which legal entity, under what current authority, against which current compliance evidence, on what exact instruction, or with what settlement and accounting outcome. We describe the ChainIT Transaction Truth Architecture, a zero-trust control, execution, and evidence architecture that places verified individual and organizational identity, the organizational authority record and authority policy of the ChainIT Authority Protocol, transaction-specific runtime compliance decisions, exact-digest approval, atomic capacity reservation, and a single-use Execution Authorization Credential in front of wallet execution, and that records settlement, reconciliation, and lifecycle evidence after the transaction. The architecture separates five boundaries: control of a key is not identity, identity is not organizational authority, authority is not compliance, compliance is not execution authority, and network confirmation is not complete commercial settlement. We describe wallet and custody profiles, including a multi-party computation (MPC) profile in which custody security is kept independent of business authority, stablecoin and Web3 evidence domains, layered finality, the U.S. stablecoin regulatory context as of September 2026, and a phased deployment in which pilot success requires that the control invariants hold under attack and failure.

Generative AI Opinion Augmentation: A Unified Multi-Agent Framework for Directional, Bidirectional, and Cross-Agent Argumentative Enrichment
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has substantially expanded the possibilities of argument generation, evidence retrieval, argument reconstruction, and human–AI collaborative reasoning. Nevertheless, adding new supporting arguments to an already expressed opinion represents a broader interaction phenomenon than conventional argument generation alone. Existing approaches predominantly examine particular tasks, such as generating arguments from statements, retrieving evidence, reconstructing missing premises, assessing argument quality, or producing counterarguments. These approaches do not necessarily establish a unified theoretical account of opinion augmentation across different agent identities, interaction directions, and collaborative configurations. This paper introduces Generative AI Opinion Augmentation (GAIOA), a proposed unified conceptual framework that defines opinion augmentation as the process through which one or more agents contribute new supporting arguments, evidence, explanations, or reasoning elements to an existing opinion while preserving its original semantic position. The framework distinguishes the identity of the opinion originator from that of the augmentation contributor, thereby allowing both entities to be the same or different agents. It encompasses human-to-human, human-to-AI, AI-to-human, AI-to-AI, and mixed multi-agent interactions, including unidirectional, bidirectional, and collective augmentation. The paper further establishes conceptual boundaries between opinion augmentation and related activities, including opinion generation, paraphrasing, summarization, counterargument generation, and opinion replacement. A multidimensional evaluation model is proposed to assess argumentative novelty, relevance, diversity, validity, opinion preservation, and augmentation contribution. In addition, the framework identifies challenges involving unsupported evidence, redundant contributions, semantic distortion, recursive augmentation, and multi-agent error propagation. To the best of the author's knowledge, this paper presents the first unified conceptual formulation specifically dedicated to directional and bidirectional opinion augmentation across human and generative-AI agents as a general interaction framework. Rather than claiming that its constituent operations have never appeared in previous research, the contribution lies in their systematic integration into a distinct, agent-independent theoretical construct. The proposed framework establishes a foundation for future computational implementation, empirical validation, and the development of more comprehensive human–AI and AI–AI argumentative interaction systems.

items.title: Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI): A Federated Identity, Trust, Attestation, and Accountability Architecture for Cross-Organization Autonomous AI Agents
items.abstract: AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations, and enforces authorization through three policy checks. We implement ATI as an external security enforcement layer that integrates with existing agent frameworks without modifying their underlying models. We evaluate ATI in a simulated federation of eight organizations using six agent frameworks, each deploying a five-agent team. Security experiments involve two organizations and assess 14 attack scenarios and six benign tasks across five agent models, using five attack variations and three repetitions per variation. A panel of judge models evaluates the experimental outcomes. With all enforcement mechanisms enabled, attack containment increases from 43% to 84% (40% to 80% for the 11 attack scenarios evaluated consistently across all configurations), while enforcement introduces approximately 174 microseconds of overhead per request. ATI is released as an open-source, framework-independent package that uses IETF WIMSE workload token formats for identity and request verification and Entity Attestation Tokens for model, tool, and system-prompt integrity verification.

items.abstract: Crypto-asset service providers increasingly meet users through websites, wallet-connect flows, and other public interfaces, but the legal duties attached to that visible layer remain fragmented across licensing, AML/CFT, marketing, consumer-protection, privacy, tax, and stablecoin regimes. Existing comparative accounts usually map regulatory perimeter and licensing architecture rather than the user-visible disclosure layer. This article maps de jure obligations and legally relevant compliance signals at the public interfaces of crypto-asset service providers across twenty-two jurisdictional units, using FATF standards and selected international policy materials as reference points. It develops a 15-category matrix that separates binding duties, conditional legal duties, inferred supervisory signals, prudential signals, and areas where no website-facing requirement was identified. The article treats the website as a regulatory disclosure interface and offers a structured starting point for jurisdiction-specific legal analysis, regulator-facing guidance, and future empirical audits of actual website compliance. A separately stated normative proposal connects consumer choice and entrepreneurial freedom to a country-of-origin regime for functionally integrated online services, with responsibility allocated across human–machine systems and agent-mediated interactions. This proposal is distinguished from the legal mapping and is not presented as an existing international exemption.
