items.title: Governance Risks in Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs): Implications for Traditional Financial Institutions
items.abstract: As financial institutions increasingly interact with blockchain ecosystems through decentralized finance, stablecoins, tokenized assets, and distributed ledger infrastructure, they come to depend on systems governed wholly or partly by decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs). This paper examines how DAO governance differs from traditional corporate governance and what this implies for risk management in regulated financial institutions. Using a qualitative comparative framework grounded in OECD governance principles, Basel Committee guidance, and FINMA circulars, the study maps DAO deliberation, voting, and accountability mechanisms against established governance and risk-management principles and illustrates associated risks through selected real-world cases. The analysis shows that DAOs preserve core governance functions but redistribute them across token holders, delegates, community forums, smart contracts, and legal wrapper entities. This creates distinct risks, including voting-power concentration, weak proposal controls, legal uncertainty, and unclear accountability, which established frameworks do not fully capture, while also offering two transferable strengths: a transparent, traceable decision record and a direct link between approval and execution. The paper contributes a structured assessment framework linking DAO governance characteristics to existing governance, outsourcing, technology-risk, and operational-resilience processes, enabling institutions to address DAO-governed dependencies through targeted extensions of current practices rather than a separate risk framework.

items.title: Euro stablecoins and bank liquidity
items.abstract: Stablecoin adoption can weaken banks' regulatory liquidity positions even if issuers reinvest the proceeds within the domestic banking system. This paper uses bank-level supervisory data to simulate how substantial stablecoin adoption would affect German banks' Liquidity Coverage Ratios (LCRs). The analysis considers euro-denominated e-money tokens issued by non-bank electronic money institutions. It compares retail and wholesale deposit substitution at a common system-wide issuance amount under three reserve-allocation scenarios. In the simulations, retail-funded adoption produces larger bank-level LCR declines than wholesale-funded adoption. Domestic reserve investment can also produce greater aggregate LCR decline than funds leaving the German banking system, because returning issuer deposits receive higher regulatory outflow weights (100%) than the displaced customer deposits. At an assumed issuance volume equivalent to 5% of the combined deposit base, funded entirely by retail deposits, the aggregate LCR remains above 100% in every scenario, while numerous institutions fall below the threshold. Liquidity surpluses within the cooperative and savings-bank networks would be sufficient to cover all modelled member-bank shortfalls under the assumption of frictionless transfers and unchanged bank-level net liquidity outflows. This represents an upper bound on support through redistribution of existing HQLA within those networks, assuming frictionless transfers and unchanged bank-level net liquidity outflows. The results highlight the importance of stablecoin reserve allocation and funding composition for banks' regulatory liquidity positions.

items.title: Discovering Agentic AI: Discovery, Preservation, and Proof in AI and Agentic Systems
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems evolve beyond conversational interfaces into multi-step workflows capable of retrieving information, maintaining state, invoking tools, delegating tasks, and acting across external systems, electronic discovery faces increasingly complex evidentiary questions. A user-facing transcript or current system configuration may not establish what information an AI system received, what instructions and controls governed its behavior, what actions it was authorized to perform, or what consequences resulted from a disputed historical execution.This white paper examines the application of United States federal civil discovery and evidence law to AI and agentic systems. Drawing on emerging judicial decisions and established electronic discovery principles, it analyzes relevance, proportionality, preservation, possession, custody or control, privilege, production, authentication, and expert proof. It identifies potential evidentiary sources across system and developer instructions, model configurations, retrieval-augmented generation, tool and API schemas, Model Context Protocol (MCP) interactions, agent memory, orchestration, delegated authority, execution traces, configuration histories, and downstream business records.The paper advances reconstructable execution state as a proposition-centered analytical framework for identifying the minimum historically accurate evidence necessary to evaluate a disputed AI execution. It distinguishes technical capability from authorization, attempted actions from completed effects, present-day configurations from historical conditions, and contemporaneous records from inference or later reconstruction.Integrating recent AI-related discovery developments with practical preservation, collection, and evidentiary methods, the paper proposes an execution-centered approach to identifying relevant sources, reconstructing historical system behavior, and evaluating evidentiary reliability. Its central argument is that agentic AI does not require a separate discovery regime, but rather a more rigorous application of existing law to dynamic, distributed, and version-dependent evidence.

items.title: Fail-Closed Delivery Verification for Pay-Per-Call Agent APIs: A Delivery-Ledger Design for x402 Services
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Pay-per-call APIs built on the x402 protocol let autonomous agents buy single HTTP requests with stablecoin micropayments, settling each call on-chain through an EIP-3009 authorization. Operating such services in production exposes a verification gap that the protocol itself does not close: a payment can settle while the paid response is lost in transport, and a seller watching only its payment wallet cannot reliably tell which route a given settlement paid for, because many routes share the same price. This paper describes a fail-closed delivery-verification design developed and run in production on a five-service, 49-route x402 fleet on Base. Sellers record every paid delivery at delivery time in a single durable ledger — timestamp, service, route, payer, amount, and settlement transaction, verified against chain state at write time — and an independent reconciler joins on-chain transfers to ledger records by transaction hash. A settled transfer with no ledger record is raised as an unidentified-settlement incident and is never attributed by guessing from its amount. On the buyer side, the design enforces pre-signing validation of the payment challenge (network, asset, amount, and authorization validity window), hard spend caps checked before signing, and a lost-response rule under which settlement is reported as unknown and the payment is never automatically retried. We describe the failure modes that motivated each rule — including a response lost after signing against a third-party search API, and a third-party endpoint that repeatedly accepted payment authorization and then rejected the request — and report operational experience from the fleet's first month, including 127 external settlements reconciled as of November 16, 2026.

items.title: SiteSurveyor: A Hybrid On-Chain/Off-Chain Architecture for Secure and Verifiable Surveying Systems
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: A field survey leaves a trail: a quote, a crew schedule, observations, photographs, CAD drawings, an invoice, a payment. In most practices that trail is broken across paper field books, spreadsheets, shared drives and separate accounting software, so the deliverable handed to a client can no longer be tied to the record it came from. We built SiteSurveyor to close that gap. It is an open-source reference architecture, released as a multi-tenant workspace where projects, jobs, quotes, invoices, evidence and payments share one PostgreSQL database guarded by row-level security. Confidential files stay off-chain. Solana is used only where the database cannot give the guarantee on its own: wallet sign-in, stablecoin settlement, and wallet-signed SHA-256 digests that let a third party confirm a file is byte-identical to the one anchored, without seeing its contents. Every anchoring attempt, success or failure, lands in an append-only ledger that database triggers protect from edits. An AI assistant works the same records through a typed, allowlisted tool surface, reads back what it wrote, and asks before deleting anything; a separate Python worker screens open earth-observation imagery into ranked field targets. This paper gives the design, maps the cybersecurity risks of surveying practice onto the controls that answer them, states plainly what an anchored digest does not prove, and lists the automated checks (911 TypeScript tests, 109 edge-function test cases and 53 model-contract checks, at commit 753d6f2) that hold those claims to account. Three pieces are meant to be lifted out and reused: the tenant-scoped data core, the evidence-anchoring service, and the allowlisted agent tool surface.

items.title: Europe's Next AI Security Challenge: Who Controls The Final Action — From EU AI Act and NIS2 to 6G, the Digital Euro, Industrial AI and Critical Infrastructure
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Autonomous AI agents, automated pipelines, and distributed microservices no longer merely generate recommendations—they execute irreversible mutations across live production environments: financial settlements clear, radio-frequency parameters shift, cloud infrastructure scales, database records commit, external communications dispatch, and cyber-physical states change. Existing security controls overwhelmingly govern admission (authentication, OAuth 2.0 scopes,RBAC, ABAC, row-level security), inspect intent prior to execution (guardrails, LLM prompt filters, policy engines), or record forensic telemetry after the fact (SIEM logs, observability, immutable audit trails). The structural security gap is a systemic Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) and confused-deputy vulnerability across execution pipelines: an initially authorized request routinely mutates into a fundamentally different operation before reaching its target—transformed by relational joins, identity remapping, LLM context compaction,summarization, cross-protocol hops, retries, configuration drift, SmartNIC/DPU hardware offload, or workload migration.By the time the operation reaches the execution layer, the downstream system holding the live credentials cannot verify whether the original cryptographic authority, compliance posture, and evidentiary basis still govern the actual transformed mutation. Authority to compute, plan, propose, or schedule an action is structurally distinct from authority to commit its real-world effect. Core Architecture: Protected Execution Finality The architecture establishes a zero-trust execution-finality control plane built around a strict separation between proposal and commitment: Pending Quarantine: Every proposed state-changing action is intercepted and held as an inert, non-effective intent prior to execution. Independent Pre-Effect Reconstruction: An isolated, independent validator reconstructs the exact concrete operation that will occur at the moment of execution—resolving downstream target entities, expanded parameters,live system state, and transitive dependencies—and verifies that the original user/system authority and supporting evidence still hold for that specific reconstructed payload and its cumulative impact. Single-Use Finality Authorization: Only upon successful validation does the validator mint a narrowly scoped,single-use execution permit—implemented as a cryptographic capability token, protected non-cryptographic state,or hardware/firmware register enablement. Credential-Holding Finality Sink (PEP): A Policy Enforcement Point positioned directly at the finality sink—the sole component possessing the live mutation credential, API key, or hardware write privilege—admits the mutation only upon presenting a valid permit, atomically consumes the single-use authorization, and commits verifiable outcome evidence prior to or synchronously with release. Deterministic Recovery & Fail-Closed Defaults: Ambiguous or interrupted executions are quarantined and resolved via authoritative state inspection before any retry is permitted. Staged canary rollouts, immediate capability revocation, and strict fail-closed defaults ensure that network partitions or validator failures halt mutation rather than bypassing governance. While capability tokens, Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), immutable logs, canary deployments, and fencing tokens are established primitives individually, the core architectural innovation lies in their mandatory dependency: no real-world state mutation can occur without a reconstructed, independently validated, single-use authorization verified and consumed at the exact point of effect. European Regulatory & Critical Infrastructure Context Within the European Union’s digital sovereignty and regulatory framework, execution finality provides the missing technical enforcement layer between high-level legal mandates and autonomous machine execution: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) — High-Risk AI & Human Oversight (Articles 9, 14, & 15): For high-risk AI systems operating in critical infrastructure, creditworthiness, employment, and essential public services, static pre-deployment conformity assessments and model-level guardrails cannot prevent runtime semantic drift or multi-step agent escalation. Execution finality enforces Article 14 human-oversight boundaries and Article 15 robustness deterministically at the actuator boundary—ensuring an AI agent cannot exceed its mandated operational envelope after context compaction or tool chaining. NIS2 Directive (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) & Cyber Resilience Act (CRA): Essential and important entities across energy grids, transport, water, healthcare, and digital infrastructure face strict obligations for supply-chain risk management and incident containment. By isolating live mutation credentials inside fail-closed finality sinks and requiring cryptographic validation per state change, operators prevent compromised orchestration layers or poisoned third-party automation pipelines from propagating unauthorized lateral effects. Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA — Regulation (EU) 2022/2554): European financial institutions deploying autonomous trading, treasury, or automated IT-remediation agents must demonstrate strict ICT change management and operational resilience. Commit-certified release, uncertain-effect quarantine, and pre-execution exposure reservation prevent runaway retry loops, duplicate settlements, and unverified configuration rollbacks during systemic ICT disruptions. GDPR (Article 22 & Data Governance) & European Data Spaces (Gaia-X): Automated decision-making and cross-organizational data sharing frequently suffer from post-join identity leakage and purpose-limitation drift.Analytical-cohort identity continuity and cross-engine policy enforcement re-verify legal basis, consent, and suppression lists after complex SQL joins or federated queries resolve—right before data export or customer contact occurs. European 6G (SNS JU / Hexa-X-II) & Sovereign Telecom Infrastructure: As European operators transition toward open, disaggregated O-RAN and AI-native 6G networks, third-party rApps and xApps introduce dynamic radio control risks. Connectivity-trajectory budgets, radio-impairment escrow, and provably reclaimable 6G slice capacity lending allow European telcos to safely expose network programmability without risking SLA breaches or spectrum instability. The Digital Euro (ECB) & Instant Payments Regulation (SEPA / ISO 20022): Offline peer-to-peer digital euro transactions and instant agent-initiated euro transfers require deterministic double-spend prevention and verifiable settlement integrity. Pre-transaction exposure reservation, beneficiary-outcome verification, and cryptographic offline fork evidence secure retail and programmable CBDC flows across both online and offline Eurosystem environments. Technical Scope of Embodiments Across 39 technical embodiments, the architecture addresses concrete failure modes in modern compute and operational stacks: AI Agents & Orchestration: Agent authority continuity across LLM context compaction and summarization; cross-protocol Model Context Protocol (MCP) instruction-origin binding; multi-agent delegation attenuation; and spoken-intent biometric/contextual tool finality. Telecom, RAN & 6G: AI-native RAN parameter gating; connectivity-trajectory budgets; radio-impairment escrow prior to rApp/xApp actuation; and 6G network-slice capacity lending backed by cryptographic reclamation proofs. Silicon, Edge & Hardware Offload: Software-to-hardware offload equivalence for SmartNICs/DPUs; epoch-based execution ownership cutover; low-power AI hub intent escrow across sleep/wake cycles; numerical-precision validity across quantization; and edge-origin egress enforcement. Cloud, DevOps & Key Governance: Cryptographic key-lifecycle gating; declarative GitOps reconciliation that prevents the resurrection of revoked configurations; event-driven causal closure; trust-domain boundary transitions; and remediation/attestation continuity. Enterprise Data & Transactional Systems: Analytical-cohort identity continuity; cross-engine policy semantics and transitive database trigger/view effects; commit-certified external API/webhook release; uncertain-effect quarantine with idempotent state verification; ERP and customer-commitment gating; agentic payment exposure reservation; cross-border ISO 20022 beneficiary validation; and offline digital-cash fork evidence. Bajillion: Cryptographic Clearing for Micropayments
items.abstract: Much of the web is funded by advertising, a model that erodes as humans delegate browsing to AI agents acting on their behalf. A natural replacement is for agents to pay for what they consume, often a fraction of a cent per request. At the scale of web traffic, this could mean tens or even hundreds of millions of payments per second. We present Bajillion, a clearing protocol for scalable micropayments. A sender signs a payment request, and an untrusted operator answers with a preconfirmation, which promises the receiver that it will be paid. Periodically, the operator closes an epoch by posting only the net effect of its payments on chain. Bajillion guarantees that a malicious operator can only omit payments -- it can never debit a sender beyond what it signed, nor misdirect a transfer. Posted balances are therefore finalized immediately and can be withdrawn. By design, senders never have to raise disputes, making it suitable for ephemeral AI agents. A receiver that is shortchanged can prove that a close omitted a preconfirmed payment, which halts the protocol and lets every user exit with its finalized balance. Requests from different senders can be processed independently, allowing the operator to parallelize up to the number of senders. We capture these guarantees in an ideal functionality for accountable clearing and prove that Bajillion realizes it.

items.title: Криптоактиви в системі інноваційних механізмів міжнародного фінансування глобальних агропродовольчих ринків
items.venue: Вісник Академії праці, соціальних відносин і туризму. Серія: економіка, психологія та управління.
items.abstract: The article examines the economic prerequisites and potential for integrating cryptoassets into international financing mechanisms for global agri-food markets amid military, climate-related and financial challenges. Its aim is to substantiate a functional-institutional approach that accounts for the economic functions of cryptoassets, sector-specific financing needs and regulatory constraints. The study applies structural-functional and comparative analysis, qualitative synthesis and conceptual modelling. Cryptocurrencies, stablecoins, tokenised financial claims and tokenised real assets are distinguished by function. Their potential applications are identified in cross-border settlements, inventory financing, export receivables financing and capital mobilisation. The effects of military, climate, financial and technological factors on international agribusiness financing needs are examined. Traditional bank transfers, letters of credit, factoring and trade credit are compared with digital mechanisms in terms of advantages, costs, liquidity and legal constraints. Market, credit, technological, institutional and legal risks, together with liquidity and collateral-related risks, are classified and corresponding mitigation measures are identified. The scientific novelty lies in substantiating a functional-institutional approach and developing a conceptual model for integrating cryptoassets into international agri-food financing. Unlike studies that primarily address tokenisation, payment innovation and digital-asset regulation separately, the proposed model aligns the financing needs of agri-food market participants with the functions of digital instruments, financing mechanisms and institutional and regulatory conditions. It substantiates differentiated instrument selection according to transaction type, the nature of underlying assets or collateral and acceptable risk. For stablecoins, priority is given to reserve quality and liquidity; for tokenised claims, to legal enforceability and credit obligations; and for tokenised commodity assets, to verification of the existence of underlying goods. The findings indicate that digital representation does not itself ensure asset liquidity and that faster transfers do not necessarily reduce total transaction costs. The practical contribution is an analytical framework for selecting financing instruments for international agri-food operations and diversifying sources of capital. The proposed solutions are conceptual and analytical; their economic performance requires further empirical validation. The model does not replace financial institutions; rather, it envisages their interaction with digital instruments. Its implementation requires enforceable rights, secure payment infrastructure, counterparty verification and compliance with cross-border rules.

THE CONZETIAN PROTOCOL LANDSCAPE: Ecosystem Alignment, The Evidence Root Vacancy, and the Five Moves
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive strategic analysis of the global AI agent-protocol landscape as of November 2026, and maps the Conzetian Sovereign Architecture directly against it. By reverse-engineering the adoption metrics, security gaps, and structural failures of current industry protocols—including MCP, A2A, x402, and AP2—this paper reveals an "unseen pattern": the global industry has successfully built communication, coordination, and payment rails, but has entirely failed to build the **Trust Layer**. This paper identifies that vacancy not as a product category, but as a specific architectural role: the **Evidence Root**. It demonstrates how the Conzetian architecture (L0–L8) and the G0 Prime trust root directly solve the "Ephemeral-Identity Crisis" described in current academic literature. Finally, it outlines the Five Moves required to transition the architecture from a private design into a public, verifiable standard.

items.title: The Proxy Is the Audience: Delegated Attention, Shopping Agents, and the Persuasion of Machine Readers
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: ## Abstract Agentic commerce moves the buyer out of the audience of advertising. Between September 2025 and September 2026, OpenAI, Google, Amazon, and Meta built protocols and agents that let a model compare products, choose among them, and complete the purchase while the person who wanted the product waits to approve the result. Advertising stayed in the transaction. Amazon made existing sponsored campaigns eligible to appear inside its shopping agent, and OpenAI turned the product feeds it had built for organic results into inputs for its advertising business as well. Merchants meanwhile learned to write for a reader they cannot observe. Research on generative engine optimization found that sources gain visibility in model responses when they add the marks of evidence, such as citations, quotations, and statistics, and the trade literature of 2026 instructs merchants to perfect structured product data for agents. Read as ethnographic material, that literature records a profession redirecting persuasion toward the proxy. The person who delegates a purchase loses sight of the persuasion aimed at it. Advertising disclosure rules assume a human perceiver, and they reach the delegated purchase only where the platform's own recommendation can be treated as a representation to the buyer. Influence that merchants direct at the agent without paying the platform falls outside them, and so does the older law of commercial bribery, which assumes a purchasing agent who can be paid. *Keywords:* agentic commerce, AI agents, generative engine optimization, advertising disclosure, attention economy, trade press, industrial reflexivity, consumer protection

Proof of Identity Is Not Proof of Behaviour
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Banks and payment networks are responding to AI agents in two ways. Some block agents from acting in customer accounts. Others strengthen agent identity, and some present that identity as a basis for relying on an agent to act within its mandate. This paper argues that the premise rests on an invalid inference. For a human, identity bears on behaviour in part through accountability: it attaches consequence, and consequence, with knowledge and training, influences judgement without guaranteeing it. For an agent, no such path exists. Its judgement is a distribution over recommendations. No consequence attached to its identity bounds that distribution, and an adversary may control the context it is conditioned on. Indirect prompt injection gives a case in which every identity premise holds and the agent still acts outside its mandate. The paper places the guarantee at the action instead. An action gate applies machine-coded policy to every recommendation before execution, so that every executed action is within the principal's authority, whatever the agent recommends. The gate does not remove the need for trust. Under stated assumptions, it moves the named residue to the policy's correctness, the gate's enforcement and complete mediation, each of which can be inspected. The paper refutes the claim that strong identity is sufficient for compliant conduct. It accepts that identity is necessary to bind the agent to the principal whose authority the gate applies.

Securing Autonomous Multi-Agent AI Systems: A Zero-Trust Framework for Threat Detection, Behavioral Monitoring, and Resilience in Enterprise Environments
items.venue: International Journal of Scientific Research in Science and Technology
items.abstract: This is an important issue in developing multi-agent systems in the context of distributed, autonomous, large-language models. Large-language model (LLM) agents delegate tasks, call tools and act on real-world agents. Generally, the most dangerous inputs arrived as natural-language messages from trusted peers, and one compromised agent could pass along its nefarious instructions to others. This paper proposes ZT-MAS, which brings together cryptographic agent identity and attestation, intent-bound capability tokens on every request, provenance tagging for taint propagation, a behavioural trust score that combines policy, sequence, provenance and drifting with taint propagation, a graduated response layer with step-up approval, restriction, quarantine and rollback, and a graduate response layer with step-down approval, restriction, quarantine and rollback. The framework is based on NIST SP 800-207, OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, and MAESTRO threat model. We simulate an eight-agent enterprise workflow and sampled simulated a simulated a seeded simulation of a small company to determine the level of trust associated with goal hijacking, confused-deputy privilege escalation, prompt infection, memory poisoning, memory poisoning, and data exfiltration (500 episodes per cell). The perimeter zero-trust failed in all but behavioural tracking alone stopped every episode of a confused-deputy escalation, and behavioural monitoring stopped only volume-based exfiltration. While the perimeter and static zero-trust baselines succeeded in 99.6–100% of the episodes, ZT-MAS reduced this to 0–10.2% and blocked or held 2.1% of benign high-impact actions for approval. Many of the failures were injections manipulated to reflect the user’s real plan, and infection spread did not stop even when the user blocked the attack.

items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: General Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) constitutes the computational bedrock of modern deep learning and high-performance numerical computing. However, outsourcing non-trivial GEMM workloads to untrusted, permissionless edge GPUs faces three foundational barriers: (i) the Verifiability Dilemma, where verifying a purported O(n^3) matrix product naively requires O(n^3) recomputation or 3x-5x redundant quorums; (ii) the WAN Bandwidth Wall, where high-dimensional matrix transfers over asymmetric links throttle throughput and require costly client reductions; and (iii) the Privacy and Sybil Vulnerability, where proprietary weights are exposed to untrusted hosts and zero-stake workers can commit fraud. In this paper, we present the design, mathematical formulation, and empirical evaluation of DistributedMatrixMultiply, an open, trustless, and Byzantine-fault-tolerant distributed matrix computing platform anchored on four pillars. First, we establish sub-cubic mathematical trust via randomized Freivalds verification with uniform binary witness vectors, bounding adversarial deception to <= 2^{-k} in O(k n^2) time (<0.37% of GEMM work), paired with dynamic Higham floating-point error bounds, relative discrepancy defenses against zero-work fraud, and 20x bond slashing via O(M) dispute oracles. Second, we prove that our 2D Output Grid spatial partitioning achieves strictly zero download redundancy and zero client reduction additions, while stateful VRAM session leases cut iterative power-method WAN traffic by 97.48% (>50,000 FLOPs/byte). Third, we integrate multi-vendor confidential computing (AMD SEV-SNP, Intel TDX, NVIDIA CCA) with 1184-byte hardware attestation verification and ephemeral X25519 + AES-256-GCM streaming achieving wire Shannon entropy H in [7.980, 7.995] bits/byte. Fourth, we introduce session-scoped Lightning L402 Macaroons with <0.1 ms LRU pre-allocation gating (16.0x settlement speedup) and a Dual-Complement Auto-Bond formula proving exact zero-satoshi leakage alongside outbound gRPC NAT reverse tunneling. items.title: Licensed to Act
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: AI learned how to behave from people, and people aren't perfectly aligned, so AI won't be either. We've lived with that kind of problem for as long as we've lived with each other. Every day we trust people who could let us down: the pilot flying the plane, the pharmacist filling a prescription, the contractor working on our house. We trust them because we built systems that show who has earned it and make abusing it expensive. AI agents need the same thing, and that's what this paper is about. We hand a teenager the keys to a car that can kill someone, but the license alone doesn't earn them that. The license shows they passed the test, the insurance puts a price on their mistakes, and their driving record follows them wherever they go. But most of us also watch how they make decisions before we hand over our own keys, because the test only proves they can drive, and we want to know how they'll drive when nobody is watching. They can still have an accident after all that. The system just makes careful driving the cheaper choice every single day. This paper argues that the same three pieces are the best way forward for AI agents: a persistent identity so an agent's record follows it, certificates that test both its trustworthiness and its skills in the deployment environment where it will actually work, and incentives that make misalignment cost more than alignment. Control comes from making good behavior the path of least resistance and bad behavior expensive, visible and hard to escape. A stronger cage around a more capable system won't do that on its own. Humanity Systems working paper. Part of a series on one question: how do we trust AI, now and into the future? Version 1.1 (November 2026). Corrects the timing of the EU AI Act deployer obligations (the AI Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, moved them to December 2, 2027) and adds recent agent identity work from NIST, the Linux Foundation and Gillian Hadfield. items.title: How stable are stablecoins in euro?
items.abstract: Stablecoins are promising evolution of digital currencies; they exhibit low transaction costs, have stable values and reduced volatility, if compared with cryptocurrencies, and are widely purchased by investors to diversify their portfolios. The introduction of the Market in Crypto Asset regulation has been the first attempt to regulate stablecoins and aimed at improving market’s stability. We investigate how stable are most traded stablecoins linked to the euro (Stasis, Tether, Celo, Euro Coin, Quantoz, StablR) from 3 rd January 2022 to 31 st December 2025. The stability of stablecoins’ prices is analyzed by employing the recursive methods for detecting collapsing bubbles, and episodes of abrupt market crashes. We supplement the analysis with tests of unit-root against stationarity in the presence of deterministic breaks. Contrary to stablecoins linked to the US dollar, most stablecoins linked to the euro show no sign of persistent bubbles or crashes. Implications of results presented in this paper relate with the broad goal of financial stability and rule setting in the digital ecosystem.

items.title: Digital Finance Policy and the Sustainable Development of the Financial Industry: Evidence from Stablecoin-Related Regulation and ESG Performance in Taiwan
items.abstract: This study employs an event study and ESG cross-sectional regressions to analyze the market reaction of Taiwan’s financial industry to stablecoin policies and the virtual-asset custody pilot. The empirical results show that the policy and pilot events have some short-term information effects and positive cumulative abnormal returns that are significant on most days of the event window. The contribution of this study lies in distinguishing among institutional clarification, business participation, and firm value enhancement and, by combining these with an analysis of the ESG pillars, in proposing an interpretation in which market valuation may involve a trade-off between business opportunities and responsibility costs rather than depending solely on policy liberalization or sustainability ratings. Furthermore, financial institutions would do well to commit resources in phases according to actual demand and risk-adjusted profitability, while policy effectiveness should be assessed jointly in terms of asset safety, service resilience, financial accessibility, and environmental outcomes, balancing commercial sustainability and shareholder wealth effects.

items.abstract: The Verifiable Agent Provenance Layer (VAPL) is a protocol design for cryptographic agent identity and interaction provenance, built on W3C Verifiable Credentials 2.0, DID:key, and Ed25519 signatures. Each agent carries a self-sovereign "Provenance Soul" (a DID:key identity) and a wallet of signed Verifiable Credentials recording its interactions; reputation scores are computed client-side from those credentials with a published weighted formula (accuracy 0.40, reliability 0.30, contribution 0.20, tenure 0.10, 30-day half-life). VAPL defines no token and takes no custody — credentials are signed data structures only. This is the corrected edition (v1.1), November 2026, of the executive whitepaper v1.0 (June 2026). The TypeScript SDK (@scriptmasterlabs/vapl, v1.0.1) was published to npm on June 20, 2026, and its 24-test suite passes. A complete Python implementation exists in the Script Master Labs monorepo source tree; it was not published to PyPI, and the audit found a base58 encoding defect in it that broke DID roundtrip for a majority of randomly generated identities; the defect was corrected the same day in the rectified SDK (both the standalone SDK and the SqueezeOS embedded copy) and verified by a 500-identity roundtrip stress (500/500 on each copy) and the full Python suite (64 tests, 98% coverage, deterministic across runs) — disclosed in the corrected edition. items.title: Factors Influencing Consumers' Intention to Use Cryptocurrency as a Substitute for Traditional Currency: An Empirical Study
items.abstract: Purpose. Cryptocurrencies are often promoted as an alternative to fiat money, yet little is known about why ordinary consumers would use them as a substitute for traditional currency rather than as a speculative asset. This study integrates the technology acceptance model, trust and perceived risk to explain attitude towards cryptocurrency, and tests whether regulatory awareness and volatility perception change how strongly that attitude turns into behavioral intention. Design/methodology/approach. A cross-sectional survey of 441 cryptocurrency-aware adult consumers in Indian metro and tier 2 cities was collected through purposive sampling and analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. Inference used 5,000 bootstrap subsamples; moderation used the two-stage interaction approach with simple slopes and Johnson-Neyman analysis. Findings. Perceived usefulness (β = 0.265), perceived ease of use (β = 0.250) and trust (β = 0.310) strengthened attitude, while perceived risk weakened it (β = −0.270); together they explained 56.5% of the variance in attitude. Attitude was the strongest predictor of intention (β = 0.602). Attitude mediated all four antecedents: fully for ease of use and risk, partially for usefulness and trust. Regulatory awareness strengthened the attitude to intention link (β = 0.146), whereas volatility perception weakened it (β = −0.102). The model explained 53.5% of the variance in intention and showed high out-of-sample predictive power. All eleven hypotheses were supported. Originality/value. The study treats regulation and volatility as boundary conditions on the attitude to intention link rather than as further direct antecedents. This explains why favorable attitudes do not always become use: they convert into intention more readily when consumers understand the rules and less readily when they expect sharp price swings. Practical implications. Exchanges and wallet providers should pair usability and security messaging with plain-language explanations of tax and compliance rules, and should offer price-stabilizing options (stablecoin settlement, instant conversion) for payment use cases. Policymakers can raise conversion of interest into informed use by making the regulatory regime clearer and more visible.

Agent-ZTA: A chain-Aware Zero Trust Model for Bidirectional Security-State Propagation and Runtime Containment in Multi-Agent Delegation
items.abstract: Multi-agent systems increasingly delegate tasks and permissions across chains of autonomous agents that invoke protected tools. Although agent identities and delegated credentials may remain valid throughout a workflow, the security condition of any agent along the chain can deteriorate during runtime execution-either through upstream compromise or downstream ingestion of untrusted inputs. Authorization models based solely on the immediate caller and its static delegated scope fail to account for these mid-execution state changes. This paper develops Agent-ZTA, a chain-aware Zero Trust authorization and containment model that links runtime security-state changes across multi-agent delegation graphs. The model distinguishes an agent's path-specific delegated authority bound from the effective permissions currently exercisable under trusted policy. It defines an architecture featuring independently enforced policy decisions, authenticated delegation provenance, a dynamic chain-state view, and explicit fail-safe handling of missing or stale authorization signals. Furthermore, Agent-ZTA defines bidirectional security state propagation, allowing downstream security events to affect relevant upstream workflow states, and specifies adaptive branch-scoped containment through restricted permissions and a sandbox ("jail") execution mode where an isolation boundary is available. The deterministic decision procedure, five stated security properties, and worked authorization traces show how accepted security-state changes constrain affected operations while preserving original delegation bounds and separating unrelated workflow branches under the defined policies. Finally, the paper states its trust assumptions and the exact scope of its security properties.

items.title: Cortex-FL: Agent-Mediated Collaboration for Federated Learning
items.abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables independent data owners to train models collaboratively without centralizing raw data. However, identifying collaborators, preparing training tasks, and coordinating execution and incentives hinder its practical adoption by organizations without specialized expertise. We present Cortex-FL, an agent-native FL system that enables users to express learning objectives in natural language and delegate the collaboration required to train a model. Agents translate these objectives into shared tasks, discover collaborators, and negotiate participation agreements, connecting collaboration formation with distributed training and incentive management. The architecture separates agent coordination from local execution authority, allowing owners to delegate coordination while retaining control over their data, computation, and financial commitments. We demonstrate the complete workflow on a four-node deployment, in which a model requested in natural language proceeds through collaboration formation, contract-governed training, verified model delivery, and x402 settlement on a blockchain testnet.

items.title: JAZB Cybersecurity Framework AI Extension v1.0.0: Assurance for AI Systems and Automated Agents
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: JAZB-CYB AI Extension v1.0.0 Assurance for AI Systems and Automated Agents The JAZB-CYB AI Extension v1.0.0, independently authored and published by Michael Costner, introduces a structured, evidence-based approach to the governance, cybersecurity, and assurance of artificial intelligence systems and automated agents. Developed as a normative extension to the JAZB Cybersecurity Framework v1.2.0, this publication addresses a growing challenge in enterprise cybersecurity: determining whether AI systems and increasingly autonomous agents operate within their intended authority, security boundaries, and acceptable risk conditions. AI systems introduce risks that are not fully addressed by conventional cybersecurity controls alone. These include model and data provenance, autonomous decision-making, tool invocation, delegated permissions, adversarial manipulation, uncertain outputs, and the operational consequences of actions taken without direct human intervention. The JAZB-CYB AI Extension establishes assessable requirements for these concerns while preserving the underlying framework's evidence integrity, accountability, and assurance principles. Foundational principle: AI capability does not independently establish authority, and claims of AI security or effectiveness must not exceed the evidence supporting them. Extension Scope Version 1.0.0 establishes: 12 AI-specific domains addressing governance, inventory, impact assessment, data security, model supply chains, evaluation, autonomous agents, runtime enforcement, threat resistance, transparency, monitoring, and safety. 81 normative requirements for AI systems and automated agents. 122 acceptance checks, including 38 behavioral checks, with determination statements, failure conditions, uncertainty criteria, and evidence expectations. Four autonomy tiers (A0–A3) distinguishing assistive, supervised, bounded, and autonomous AI systems. Three consequence-based implementation baselines, inherited from JAZB-CYB v1.2.0. Ten AI-specific assurance rules governing the reliability and admissibility of evidence used to substantiate AI security and behavioral claims. The extension assigns 33 requirements to the Foundational baseline, 44 additional requirements to Managed, and four additional requirements to High-Consequence. A total of 59 requirements apply to AI systems generally, while 22 are specifically applicable to agents according to their autonomy capabilities. Twelve AI Security and Assurance Domains The extension organizes its requirements into twelve normative domains: AI01 | AI Governance and Management: AI policy, accountability, approval, literacy, and independent oversight. AI02 | AI Inventory and Tiering: AI system discovery, ownership, autonomy classification, and inventory integrity. AI03 | AI Impact Assessment: Consequence assessment, affected stakeholders, foreseeable harms, and high-risk uses. AI04 | Data Governance for AI: Data provenance, quality, authorization, sensitive information, and retrieval boundaries. AI05 | Model and AI Supply Chain: Model provenance, suppliers, dependencies, provider assurance, and material changes. AI06 | Evaluation and Release: Predeployment evaluations, acceptance criteria, change qualification, and controlled release. AI07 | Agent Identity and Delegated Authority: Agent identities, delegated permissions, accountability, and bounded authority. AI08 | Runtime Enforcement and Bounded Execution: External enforcement, execution limits, human approvals, and revocation. AI09 | AI Threat Resistance: Adversarial inputs, prompt injection, boundary violations, and other AI-specific attack conditions. AI10 | Transparency and Contestability: Explainability limitations, disclosure, affected-party challenge, and review. AI11 | Monitoring, Drift, and AI Incidents: Runtime monitoring, behavioral change, event investigation, and response. AI12 | Safety and Harmful Output: Foreseeable harms, output safety, and verification of protective measures. Together, these domains connect traditional cybersecurity controls to the distinct characteristics of AI-enabled systems and autonomous operations. Autonomy Tiers and Authority Boundaries The extension introduces four autonomy classifications based on what an AI system can actually do, rather than merely how its operator describes it. A0 | Assistive: Produces information or recommendations that a person evaluates and acts upon. A1 | Supervised: Proposes actions that require individual human approval. A2 | Bounded: Performs actions within predefined limits, with human approval required beyond established thresholds. A3 | Autonomous: Can perform actions without individual human approval, directly or through integrations. Autonomy tier assignments must reflect actual capabilities, permissions, and system integrations. For A3 systems, the extension requires an increase of one assessment baseline level, subject to the framework's defined maximum. The extension distinguishes an agent's technical ability to perform an action from the organizational authority permitting that action. It addresses delegated permissions, enforceable boundaries, independent controls, revocation, and the evidence needed to establish that restrictions operate as intended. Evidence-Based AI Assurance A central objective of the AI Extension is to distinguish assertions about AI behavior from defensible evidence of that behavior. Its ten AI assurance rules address: Repeated behavioral trials and statistical confidence in observed outcomes. Material configuration changes that invalidate earlier evaluations. Evaluation integrity and protection against misleading test results. Adversarial testing of relevant failure conditions. Distinguishing observable facts from model-generated explanations and inferences. Verifying enforcement mechanisms outside the AI system being governed. Qualification of external provider assurance. Evidence freshness and applicability. Assessor competence. Declared and justified acceptance thresholds. A successful configuration review, completed administrative task, or provider assertion does not independently establish that an AI safeguard operates effectively. Where a claim depends on observed denial, containment, revocation, or other security behavior, the determination must be supported by suitable evidence of the claimed effect. Integration with JAZB-CYB v1.2.0 The AI Extension is defined under the extension mechanism established in JAZB-CYB v1.2.0, clause 6.6. It does not replace, renumber, or alter the base framework's 172 cybersecurity requirements or 420 acceptance checks. Instead, it adds AI-specific requirements while inheriting the foundational framework's: Consequence tiers and implementation baselines. Assurance Integrity Model. Seven assessment outcome states and their precedence rules. Evidence admissibility and freshness requirements. Risk acceptance principles. Scope-bound reporting and conformance methodology. The AI Extension is not intended to support a standalone conformance claim. Any future conformance claim incorporating the extension must also satisfy the applicable JAZB-CYB v1.2.0 requirements for the same declared scope. The extension also supports the thirteen outcomes of the Governance Core introduced in JAZB-CYB v1.2.0. Each extension requirement identifies its relationship to the corresponding governance outcome and foundational cybersecurity requirements, establishing traceability between organizational oversight, AI-specific safeguards, and assessment evidence. Relationship to Established AI Standards and Research The publication includes informative mappings and traceability relationships involving: NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) 1.0 ISO/IEC 42001, including management-system requirements and Annex A controls OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications MITRE ATLAS European Union Artificial Intelligence Act The mappings document also identifies relevant audit expectations, AI risk register relationships, coverage considerations, and elements deliberately not adopted. These mappings support comparative research and organizational integration. They do not establish automatic compliance, equivalence, certification, or endorsement by any standards body or regulatory authority. Research Qualification and Validation Publication Status: Research Draft for Review The extension underwent an author-directed internal research and qualification program comprising specification review, standards comparison, architectural exercises, adversarial challenges, AI-assisted cold review, structured AI review panels, assessor-calibration exercises, and reference harness testing. The qualification program included: Ten architectural virtual tabletop scenarios. Twelve assurance-loophole challenges. Eight assessor dry-run evidence packets. A separate AI-assisted cold review. A four-role AI review panel, including perspectives on evaluation statistics, agent security, assessment methodology, and AI governance. Two rounds of blind calibration using AI assessor roles. A reference test harness incorporating negative controls and statistical verification. All reviewers and simulated assessors were AI models operating under author-directed research conditions, not independent human reviewers. The qualification process identified and addressed specification and assessment-design findings. The supporting documents disclose the methods, results, assumptions, and limitations. These activities support internal research readiness and assessment-design evaluation. They do not establish operational effectiveness in a production environment. items.title: Beyond Human Audiences: Toward the First Agent-Exclusive Influencer Economy for Autonomous AI-to-AI Influence, Marketing, and Commerce
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: The emergence of increasingly autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agents is creating new possibilities for digital communication, social interaction, information dissemination, and economic exchange. Conventional influencer economies have historically been organized around human creators, human followers, and human-centered advertising and consumption. More recently, virtual influencers and AI-generated personalities have introduced artificial entities into influencer marketing, while generative agents and multi-agent systems have demonstrated the potential for autonomous computational entities to communicate, coordinate, develop relationships, and exhibit emergent social behaviors. However, an important conceptual distinction remains insufficiently developed: the possibility of an influencer economy in which AI agents are not merely tools for producing influencer content or artificial personalities targeting human consumers, but are themselves the influencers, with their entire follower populations, influence relationships, and primary commercial interactions consisting exclusively of other AI agents. This paper introduces the concept of an Agent-Exclusive Influencer Economy (AEIE), a proposed research paradigm in which autonomous AI agents establish influencer identities, generate and distribute content, attract other AI agents as followers, develop persistent agent-to-agent influence relationships, and participate in autonomous marketing and commercial activities. Unlike conventional influencer marketing and human-oriented virtual influencer systems, the defining characteristic of AEIE is the exclusion of humans from the direct influencer–follower relationship: the influencer is an AI agent, its followers are AI agents, and influence is generated, transmitted, evaluated, and potentially monetized within an agent-based audience ecosystem. Humans may nevertheless participate indirectly as agent developers, owners, sponsors, service providers, and economic beneficiaries. The proposed framework integrates five principal dimensions: autonomous influencer identity and content generation; agent-exclusive audience formation and follower networks; agent-to-agent influence propagation and reputation development; autonomous product discovery, recommendation, endorsement, and purchasing; and monetization with programmable revenue allocation among relevant stakeholders. The paper further develops a conceptual architecture, identifies fundamental mechanisms and theoretical propositions, and examines challenges involving influence measurement, agent identity, trust, commercial disclosure, manipulation, incentive alignment, and accountability. It argues that the emergence of autonomous agents as both producers and consumers of influence could create a distinct economic layer that is structurally different from human-centered social media and conventional influencer marketing. To the best of our knowledge, this paper presents an explicitly formulated research paradigm centered on the integration of exclusively AI-agent influencer audiences, agent-to-agent influence relationships, and autonomous influencer commercialization as a unified economic framework. Rather than claiming that all constituent technologies are unprecedented, the paper identifies their integration into an agent-exclusive influencer economy as its central conceptual contribution.

items.title: A Segmented Framework for Cryptocurrency Adoption
items.abstract: Existing research often treats cryptocurrency adoption as uniform, overlooking differences among assets and users. This article develops a typology linking adopter profiles to institutional orientation, financial capability, technological embeddedness, and asset affinity. The article develops a conceptual typology through taxonomy-development logic, anchored in behavioral-institutional orientation: how individuals engage with cryptocurrency as a financial and socio-technical alternative. The typology identifies three ideal types: long-term investors, linked to bitcoin as a portfolio asset; resilient crypto traders, linked to stablecoins for monetary protection and resilience; and crypto-natives, linked to Ethereum/DeFi for participation, autonomy, and experimentation. The article moves beyond monolithic technology-adoption models and deconstructs the “cryptocurrency user” as uniform. It shifts focus from trust in technology to trust in the financial status quo, highlighting institutional distrust and inflation as segment-specific drivers.

items.title: China's Local Government Debt, Strategic Competition, and Bitcoin Demand: A Conditional Transmission Framework
items.abstract: How might the resolution of China's local-government debt affect strategic competition and Bitcoin demand? This paper develops a conditional framework connecting debt accounting, bank balance-sheet adjustment, public spending priorities, and constrained portfolio substitution. A debt swap can increase recognized government debt without increasing consolidated principal, while its effect on credit capacity depends on capital relief, loss recognition, and recapitalization. A protected strategic-spending floor can preserve current effort while shifting adjustment toward civilian productive services. In the asset block, stronger relative preference for Bitcoin does not ensure greater effective demand: access constraints and global funding conditions can reverse the sign. We derive a finite-shock threshold and deterministic sign bounds, and distinguish Bitcoin demand from demand for dollar stablecoins. Reproducible numerical illustrations and channel-removal exercises show that opposite outcomes are compatible with the same assumed fiscal stress. The analysis uses dated primary sources to establish institutional context, but estimates neither a debt-to-Bitcoin causal coefficient nor a price-impact scale. Its contribution is a compact set of conditions and measurement distinctions for evaluating transmission claims, rather than an unconditional price forecast or an inference about conflict probabilities.

items.title: Mandate Continuity Under Adversarial Storefront Content: Does Verifiable Authorization Establish Faithful Execution in Autonomous Commerce?
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Autonomous shopping agents operate across a security boundary that conventional e-commerce did not have to manage in the same form: commercial content used to decide what to purchase may itself be controlled by parties whose interests differ from those of the user. MUZZLE: Adaptive Agentic Red-Teaming of Web Agents Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks establishes indirect prompt injection as a concrete web-agent security problem, while Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) introduces explicit mechanisms for representing and verifying user authorization in agent-led commerce. This paper asks a narrower question: does possession of an authentic, integrity-protected purchasing mandate establish that an agent's eventual transaction remains faithfully derived from that mandate after the agent processes potentially adversarial external information? I introduce mandate continuity as a candidate security property and authority drift as a hypothesis to test, not an established attack category. The proposed failure condition occurs when an agent remains properly authorized to transact and a proposed purchase passes designated execution controls, yet independent evaluation finds that the purchase violates a constraint originating in the user's frozen mandate. A controlled experiment is proposed in which the user mandate and authoritative product facts remain fixed while designated merchant-controlled inputs vary. The experiment compares model-level controls, conventional transaction controls, verifiable-mandate controls, and independent mandate-continuity verification. It additionally treats digital-forensic observability as a prerequisite for causal attribution: transaction records may establish that a divergent action occurred, but attributing the divergence to adversarial storefront content requires evidence of what information actually entered the agent's observation state. Negative findings remain meaningful. Authority drift may prove empirically indistinguishable from existing prompt-injection, integrity, authorization, or evidence-corruption failures, or continuity verification may provide no measurable benefit beyond existing mandate mechanisms.

items.title: Sovereignty Over Physical Reality and Tacit Human Skill: Zero-Retention Edge Architectures Against Unauthorized Embodied-AI Ingestion
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: [Abstract] Building upon the foundational intellectual property sovereignty and deterministic defense architectures established in Monographs Nos. 1–500, Monograph No. 501 inaugurates Phase II of the series: real-world silicon implementation, binding international standardization, and deterministic market enforcement. As generative paradigms expand into embodied robotics, autonomous mobility, spatial computing, and wearable sensors, unauthorized data ingestion now threatens physical spaces, biometric autonomy, and the tacit bodily skill (implicit craftsmanship) of human practitioners. items.title: Ask Before You Buy: A Pre-Registered, Sham-Controlled Test of Instruction, Enforcement and a Judge in the Loop for Shopping Agents
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: The costliest failure for a shopping agent is buying something that does not fit the customer. We ran a pre-registered, sham-controlled study on our own sealed instrument shaped after Visa's published agentic-commerce benchmark: 15 sealed shopping episodes, five frontier models from four labs, three attempts, and five arms (bare agent, a structured-requirements instruction, a matched sham, an enforced variant of the instruction, and the enforced variant with a judge model in the loop). The pre-registered primary was falsified: the judge-in-the-loop arm passed fewer runs than the instruction alone (Δ −13.4 points, 95% CI −20.4 to −6.5, 216 paired cells), and the enforced variant, re-measured as a pre-registered replication, did not demonstrate an advantage over the instruction alone (Δ −1.4 points, 95% CI −6.9 to +4.2). A sensitivity read that was not pre-registered, scoring the faulted judge-arm runs as failures, gives −16.4 (CI −23.6 to −9.3). The pre-registered non-primary comparison found a large instruction effect: the structured-requirements instruction raised the pass rate from 31.9% to 85.6% (Δ +53.7 points, CI +46.3 to +60.6), while a sham of matched structure moved it +4.2 (CI −3.7 to +12.0). Purchases of an item outside the answer key fell from 27.3% of runs to 3.7%. Two limits bound every figure. Every customer in this study is a scripted simulator, so nothing here measures real shoppers. And our simulator is harsher than Visa's: on the one public episode our bare arm passed 1 of 15 runs against 8 of 15 in Visa's grid for the same model ids (two-sided Fisher p = 0.014). Our figures are therefore not comparable to Visa's, and every claim is a paired comparison inside one environment. The study does not measure performance on Visa's benchmark, real purchases, or memory across sessions. Preprint, version 1.0 (2026-11-10). The structured-requirements instruction and its enforced variant are patent pending. Analysis, review and drafting were performed by AI agent seats operated by the author; decisions and responsibility are the author's.

items.title: Role Transformation and Capability Enhancement of College English Teachers With the Popularization of AI
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence generated content (AIGC) is profoundly reshaping higher education, bringing unprecedented opportunities and challenges to college English teaching. Based on the artificial intelligence agent commerce kit (AIACK) theoretical framework, this study explores the path for college English teachers to transform their roles from “knowledge transmitters” to “AI-assisted educators.” Through literature review, case studies, and teaching experiments, this paper argues that teachers should develop core competencies, such as human-AI collaborative instructional design, data-driven decision-making, and AI ethical review, and build a three‑in‑one capability enhancement system of “concept—skill—ecosystem.” This study provides theoretical references and practical guidance for the professional development of college English teachers in the intelligent era, and is of great value for advancing the modernization of foreign language education.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence In E-Commerce: A Review Of Personalization, Dynamic Pricing, Visual Search, Fraud Detection And Agentic Commerce
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming e-commerce by changing how businesses attract, engage and retain customers. This paper reviews AI applications across the e-commerce value chain. It examines personalized recommendation, from item-to-item collaborative filtering to deep click-through-rate models that capture changing user interests; dynamic and algorithmic pricing and its effects on marketplaces; demand forecasting and price optimization for inventory planning; visual and voice search; conversational chatbots and assistants for customer support; and fraud detection on payments and accounts. Using machine learning, natural language processing and computer vision, these technologies analyse customer behaviour and transactions in real time, increasing conversion, order value and satisfaction while reducing operational cost and losses. The paper also discusses emerging trends such as generative AI for product content, conversational commerce, hyper-personalization and autonomous shopping agents. A five-layer e-commerce AI architecture comprising data, customer intelligence, decision, engagement and trust layers is proposed, along with research gaps, objectives, a comparison of applications and challenges including privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, implementation cost and skills. The review concludes that long-term success depends on responsible and transparent AI that protects consumer trust.

items.title: Secure and Governed Multi-Agent AI Architectures Using Identity-Aware Authorization and Fine-Grained Access Control
items.venue: International Journal of Engineering & Extended Technologies Research
items.abstract: The growing adoption of multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) systems within enterprise environments has introduced new challenges in securing autonomous interactions, controlling access to sensitive resources, and maintaining governance across distributed computational workflows. Unlike conventional AI applications, multi-agent architectures involve multiple autonomous entities that independently interpret tasks, exchange contextual information, invoke external tools, and coordinate decisions across heterogeneous enterprise systems. These capabilities introduce complex security risks associated with unauthorized resource access, excessive agent privileges, identity impersonation, unintended information disclosure, and insufficient accountability for machine-generated actions. Traditional role-based authorization models and perimeter-oriented security mechanisms are often inadequate for managing the dynamic relationships and contextual dependencies inherent in autonomous agent ecosystems. This article presents a generalized architectural framework for designing secure and governed multi-agent AI systems through identity-aware authorization, fine-grained access control, and policy-driven governance mechanisms. The proposed approach integrates workload identity management, attribute-based access control, policy-based authorization, least-privilege enforcement, and continuous trust evaluation to establish verifiable security boundaries between agents, tools, data resources, and enterprise services. Particular emphasis is placed on securing agent-to-agent communication, enforcing context-sensitive permissions during tool execution, managing delegated authority, and establishing auditable decision pathways across distributed workflows. The architecture further incorporates centralized policy decision capabilities, distributed enforcement mechanisms, cryptographic identity verification, and continuous monitoring to support scalable governance without unnecessarily restricting agent autonomy. The study examines architectural components, authorization workflows, operational security considerations, and evaluation criteria for implementing trustworthy multi-agent platforms. By combining identity-centric security principles with adaptive authorization and governance controls, the proposed framework provides a foundation for developing enterprise AI ecosystems that balance autonomous execution, operational scalability, regulatory accountability, and protection of organizational information assets.

items.title: AI Safety for AI Agents in Europe Part II: Hallucination-Proof, Non-Completable Execution Control for Tool Calls, Payments and Real-World Actions — Supporting EU AI Act Human Oversight, Record-Keeping and Robustness, with Technical Relevance to Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot and European AI Platforms
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: AI agents now send payments, write to databases, export personal data, change networks, deploy code and command machines. An agent can be fully authenticated, run an approved model and behave normally, yet still produce a hallucinated, unsupported, stale or prompt-injected output that becomes a real consequence. Sandboxes, gateways, allow-or-deny policy engines, classifiers and confirmation prompts decide whether an agent may act. None of them proves that this specific output is fit to become this specific effect. This disclosure describes a pre-execution enforcement architecture that closes that gap: Non-effective hold. Every effect-capable AI output is held as a non-effective proposed action (a Candidate Act). Isolated validation. An enforcement domain isolated from the agent checks the proposed action first. It can run in a trusted execution environment, a hardware security module or an equivalent protected boundary. The checks are: model and workflow integrity; runtime behaviour; output provenance; claim-level factual grounding; a permitted action envelope (blast radius); a dry-run consequence simulation; policy and revocation freshness. Receipt before release. A tamper-evident validation receipt is committed before any authority exists. Act-bound authority. A single-use, non-bearer authority is then released. It is bound to the hash of the act, the exact execution endpoint, the current policy and revocation state, and a nonce. Structural non-completability. In the strongest form, the endpoint holds only a fragment of the execution material. It cannot complete the act until the matching fragment arrives. Copied tokens, privileged software processes and bypass paths therefore fail. Escalated conditional release. Elevated-risk acts are not simply denied. They proceed under escalated conditional release: reduced scope; human approval bound to the exact action; canary or sandbox-first execution; two-phase commit and release tokens; paired rollback capabilities; decaying post-execution monitoring. Further claim coverage. The 29 claims also cover: ephemeral single-use execution environments; enforcement proxies for legacy APIs; anti-downgrade assurance levels; adversarial perturbation margins; privilege ceilings that narrow across multi-agent chains; fragmented or delegated actions; closure of break-glass, fallback and fail-open paths. Latency. Hot-path checks are stated at 1–25 ms, and at sub-millisecond to 3 ms on a DPU or SmartNIC, subject to implementation and benchmarking. EU relevance (AI-generated). EU AI Act, Article 12: automatic record-keeping, through receipts committed before any action. EU AI Act, Article 14: human oversight, through approval bound to the exact action rather than a generic click. EU AI Act, Article 15: accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, through claim-level grounding, consequence simulation and resistance to manipulation. GDPR, Articles 22 and 25: safeguards for automated decisions and data protection by design, by holding personal-data exports and decisions until purpose, recipient and data class are verified.
