items.title: When AI Agents Call, Message, Book and Pay: Privacy-Preserving Virtual Identities and Hardware-Bound Consent Enforcement for Autonomous Commerce and Global Digital Communications
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: TECHNICAL DISCLOSURE — PRIVACY-PRESERVING IDENTITY FOR AI AGENTS AND DIGITAL COMMERCE Abstract As artificial intelligence evolves toward autonomous agents capable of contacting businesses, booking travel, exchanging messages, negotiating services, and executing payments, the protection of permanent personal identifiers is becoming a significant challenge for digital trust, privacy engineering, and secure AI-driven commerce. Each commercial interaction may expose telephone numbers, email addresses, payment identifiers, or other persistent identity information to external businesses, communication providers, and intermediary platforms. Existing technologies—including temporary phone numbers, masked email addresses, communication relays, payment tokenization, and consent-management systems—provide important privacy protections. However, a temporary identifier does not necessarily establish that every subsequent communication, transaction, or cross-border transfer remains authorized for the original session, recipient, jurisdiction, and purpose. This technical disclosure presents a proposed cryptographically enforced, session-scoped Virtual Identity (VI) and Compliance Jurisdiction Token (CJT) architecture, described in published international patent application PCT/IB2025/058743 (WO2025210622A2), for protecting personal identity during commercial communications and transactions. The architecture introduces a Virtual Identity Engine that substitutes permanent identifiers—including telephone numbers, email addresses, VoIP identities, messaging handles, and selected financial references—with session-specific pseudonymous identities. A Hybrid Virtual Identity (HVI) supports the protected association of multiple identifiers within a defined commercial interaction. Each VI or HVI is bound to a Compliance Jurisdiction Token (CJT) or Hybrid CJT (HCJT) containing session identity, validity, jurisdictional restrictions, authorization or consent evidence, and cryptographic anti-replay information. Protected identity-mapping and verification operations are performed within a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) or Hardware Security Module (HSM). A Gateway Enforcement Module (GEM) verifies the relevant VI–CJT binding before permitting a controlled communication or transaction operation. Potential enforcement environments include SIP/VoIP gateways, WebRTC services, email relays, commercial messaging infrastructure, API gateways, financial transaction processors, and selected satellite communication systems. Signed revocation artifacts, session expiry, and tamper-evident audit records provide additional mechanisms for limiting unauthorized reuse and supporting independent verification. Further embodiments address advertiser-origin binding, isolation of commercial leads across businesses, virtual-number misuse, caller-ID spoofing, one-time callbacks, jurisdiction-aware data routing, Virtual Finance Cards, payment authorization, and financial compliance-related verification. European and International Research Relevance The architecture is relevant to research concerning trustworthy AI, privacy by design, digital sovereignty, pseudonymous identity, secure communication, consent management, and cross-border data governance. In a European context, the proposed mechanisms may support technical objectives associated with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), particularly data minimization, purpose limitation, data protection by design, and international-transfer safeguards. The architecture may also be relevant to secure electronic communications, financial technology, and trusted digital-service infrastructure. Cryptographic validation of an authorization record does not independently establish the legal validity of consent or compliance with international data-transfer requirements. Regulatory applicability and compliance must be assessed separately. Big Tech Technical Relevance and Future Product Alignment The proposed architecture may complement existing product ecosystems associated with: Apple: Hide My Email, private communication relays, Apple Pay, and secure device infrastructure, through more granular session- and purpose-bound identity controls. Google: Gemini-powered business interactions, Google Ads, Google Voice, and Google Cloud, through protected commercial identities, advertiser-specific authorization, and controlled communication gateways. Meta: WhatsApp Business, Messenger, Facebook and Instagram Lead Ads, through session-specific customer-contact references that limit unauthorized cross-business reuse. OpenAI and Anthropic: ChatGPT agents, OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude, Claude Code, and MCP-connected services, through protected identities for agent-initiated messaging, bookings, external communications, and commercial transactions. Microsoft: Copilot, Azure Communication Services, Teams Phone, and enterprise data infrastructure, through cryptographically verifiable communication scope and jurisdiction-aware authorization. Amazon Web Services and Twilio: Protected identity processing, programmable communication services, masked contact systems, and verification APIs. Booking.com and other digital marketplaces: Session-bound guest or customer contact references that preserve legitimate commercial communication without routinely disclosing permanent personal identifiers. Visa, Mastercard, Stripe, and financial infrastructure providers: Virtual payment credentials, merchant-scoped authorization, and protected transaction-specific identity verification. Nokia, Qualcomm, and telecommunications operators: Protected communication gateways, trusted device processing, programmable network services, and potentially future AI-native 6G communication environments. These relationships represent potential technical integration opportunities, not confirmed company implementations or roadmap commitments. Scientific and Industrial Significance The central technical contribution is a proposed integration of ephemeral identity substitution, cryptographically bound authorization, protected verification, gateway-level enforcement, revocation, and verifiable audit evidence across heterogeneous digital communication and transaction systems. As AI agents increasingly interact with businesses on behalf of users, the architecture offers a potential mechanism for separating the authority to perform a specific task from unrestricted access to a person's permanent identity. Core principle: An AI agent may communicate, book, purchase, or transact on behalf of a user without automatically disclosing permanent identifiers or granting unlimited future contact authority. The disclosure offers a possible foundation for privacy-preserving agentic commerce, interoperable digital identity, secure communications, and jurisdiction-aware processing. Its technical performance, enforcement coverage, security advantages, and integration feasibility require independent experimental validation. items.title: AI Safety for AI Agents in Europe Part IV : Two Independent Checks and Endpoint-Side Reconstruction to Prevent Tool Misuse, Memory Poisoning, Unauthorized Delegation and Unlawful Data Use — Supporting EU AI Act Record-Keeping, Human Oversight and Cybersecurity, GDPR Purpose Limitation and DORA
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Abstract In most AI-agent and automation stacks, one component decides and a downstream component simply trusts that decision. A policy engine, gateway, classifier, trusted execution environment or approval step says yes. The tool, MCP server, database, cloud API or payment rail then carries out whatever request arrives with that approval. This leaves several gaps: the checker may be the same component that collected the inputs; approvals, tokens and receipts can be replayed, widened, rerouted or used after policy has changed; the operation that was checked can differ from the one actually committed, a time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap; personal and enterprise data, once readable, can be indexed, embedded, joined, exported, used for training or used to steer an agent without any explicit authorization for that use. Under GDPR purpose limitation and the EU AI Act’s expectations for oversight and cybersecurity, these gaps are exactly where controls are needed. Today they are mostly covered by policy, logging and after-the-fact audit. This disclosure describes a two-instance execution-control architecture that removes the single point of trust: First check, at collection time. A first protected domain binds inputs, instructions, provenance, purpose, jurisdiction, scope and permitted effect when the data arrives. An input integrity gateway seals provenance first, so poisoned inputs are refused binding. Second, independent check, at execution time. A second protected domain validates the proposed action against that binding. It is independent through a separate hardware root, session, keys, runtime or administration. It produces evidence cross-committed to the binding, so neither artifact alone can authorize anything. Release only on agreement. Only when both artifacts mutually corroborate is a single-use, non-bearer authority released. The endpoint checks what is actually happening. At the execution boundary, the endpoint independently reconstructs the actual pending operation through its own attested observation channel. Endpoints include: a tool dispatcher, MCP or connector gateway, or API gateway; a database commit or cloud control plane; cross-border data egress, a payment rail or an actuator. What the endpoint reconstructs. It reconstructs recipient, purpose, jurisdiction, data category and the actual operation. It checks these against both artifacts and against its own state (nonce, counter, spent-capability, and its own policy and revocation epochs). Atomic commit. The endpoint commits the operation atomically, as exactly the operation it verified. Contained compromise. A compromise of either domain, the transport channel or the compute plane is confined to its own window and cannot by itself make an unauthorized act effective. Mismatches fail closed before the effect, not through rollback afterwards. Readable but inert data. Data, agent memories and retrieved documents can remain stored and readable while staying operationally inert. They cannot be indexed, embedded, exported, served, used for training or used to influence a tool call unless that specific use is authorized. Chained evidence. Evidence produced at the endpoint becomes a required input to the next step, and chained validation receipts provide a verifiable record at every point. Shared, not central, authority. Distributed partial shares can replace any central authority, so no single party ever holds a complete reusable authorization. The 54 claims, 15 of them independent, cover: AI-agent tool dispatch; MCP and connector supply-chain substitution; computer-use and browser actions; memory and RAG inertness; multi-agent delegation chains; autonomous cloud-control changes; regulated AI output release by purpose, jurisdiction and recipient; coding and CI/CD agents; agent skills and marketplace extensions; multimodal assistants; voice and meeting agents with consent and recording checks; agentic purchasing; persistent AI memory; workspace and scheduled agents. EU AI Act, Article 14 (human oversight): approval evidence that must corroborate an independent check, and is verified at the point of effect. items.abstract: AI agents now send payments, write to databases, export personal data, change networks, deploy code and command machines. An agent can be fully authenticated, run an approved model and behave normally, yet still produce a hallucinated, unsupported, stale or prompt-injected output that becomes a real consequence. Sandboxes, gateways, allow-or-deny policy engines, classifiers and confirmation prompts decide whether an agent may act. None of them proves that this specific output is fit to become this specific effect. This disclosure describes a pre-execution enforcement architecture that closes that gap: Non-effective hold. Every effect-capable AI output is held as a non-effective Candidate Act. Isolated validation. An enforcement domain isolated from the agent checks it first. The checks cover model and workflow integrity, runtime behaviour, output provenance, claim-level factual grounding, a permitted action envelope (blast radius), a dry-run consequence simulation, and policy and revocation freshness. Receipt before release. A tamper-evident validation receipt is committed before any authority exists. Act-bound authority. A single-use, non-bearer authority is then released. It is bound to the act’s hash, the exact execution endpoint, the current policy and revocation state, and a nonce. Structural non-completability. In the strongest form, the endpoint holds only a fragment of the execution material. It cannot complete the act until the matching fragment arrives, so copied tokens, privileged software and bypass paths fail. Escalated release. Elevated-risk acts are not simply denied. They proceed under escalated release: reduced scope, human approval bound to the exact action, canary or sandbox-first execution, two-phase commit and release tokens, or paired rollback capabilities. items.title: The rise of the agent economy: Autonomous agent organizations as a new form of economic infrastructure
items.abstract: This paper examines autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agents and the emerging agent economy through a case study of the blockchain-based Virtuals Protocol. It analyzes how tokenized ownership, decentralized governance, and standardized coordination support economic organization in multi-agent systems. Drawing on transaction cost economics and network economics, the study identifies mechanisms through which the protocol may reshape coordination costs and support network effects through agent specialization and composability. The concept of Autonomous Agent Organizations (AAOs) is introduced as a functional subclass of Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs), distinguished by their greater economic autonomy and composable inter-agent collaboration. AAOs represent a novel form of economic organization that transcends traditional boundaries between firms, markets, and platforms. The findings have practical implications for platform design, governance, and regulatory development. The study contributes to research on agentic AI and digital platform governance by explaining how agent autonomy, tokenized ownership, and protocol-based coordination shape emerging forms of economic organization.

items.title: ANOA — Essay XV: The Axiomatic Theory of Distributed Monetary Circulation in AI-Native Economies
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: ANOA — Essay XV: The Axiomatic Theory of Distributed Monetary Circulation in AI-Native Economies This independent theoretical research manuscript develops an axiomatic and technology-neutral framework for monetary circulation in AI-native economies characterized by autonomous economic agents, federated infrastructures, endogenous bank credit, and heterogeneous monetary institutions. The study distinguishes monetary creation, payment instructions, agentic asset allocation, inferential market access, liquidity provisioning, and legally final settlement. It develops stock-flow-consistent accounting constructions and conditional propositions addressing commercial bank money creation, interbank settlement, foreign-exchange transactions, collateral constraints, synchronized agentic payment demand, and network-dependent monetary policy transmission. A central contribution is the separation of programmable money, conditional payments, programmable settlement infrastructures, and mandate-bound agentic spending. The manuscript compares conventional banking infrastructures, central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), tokenized deposits, stablecoins, federated non-DLT systems, and blockchain-based architectures without presuming that AI-native economic coordination requires a new universal currency or a mandatory distributed ledger. The research integrates conceptual foundations from the ANOA and HomeSelf Research corpus, including global protocol federalism, distributed macroeconomic equilibrium, cyber-physical stability, computational production, systemic resilience, inferential scarcity, and agentic asset allocation. Its constitutional framework emphasizes human sovereignty, monetary pluralism, institutional accountability, lawful settlement, contestable economic access, and technological proportionality. The mathematical results are conditional on explicitly stated accounting, institutional, and behavioral assumptions. The manuscript does not claim empirical validation, regulatory authorization, institutional endorsement, or the issuance of a new monetary instrument. items.title: The General Transaction Layer for AI Agents: Why Verifiable Agent Commerce Is a Special Case of Verifiable Agent Action, and What the General Case Requires
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: AI agents are beginning to act with real authority—to buy, approve, file, escalate, and decide on a person’s or an organization’s behalf. The payments industry has recognized that such actions require verifiable authorization and a tamper-proof record, and in 2026 moved to standardize exactly that for one verb: pay. This note argues that payment is a special case of a more general problem—any consequential agent action needs the same discipline—and that the general case has structure the payment case can leave implicit: pre-execution policy admission, outcome verification against declared criteria, and a portable, cross-implementation evidence record not bound to any single platform or rail. We describe the Trusted Cognitive Execution Architecture (TCEA) as a reference design for that general layer, map the agent-payment mandate chain onto it as a special case, and argue that the general agent-action governance layer is, as of this writing, named as a need by emerging standards work and not yet claimed by any published consortium scope. This note states the position; an open reference implementation and specification corpus follow.

items.title: Signed Is Not the Same as Behaving the Same: Algorithmic Logic Fingerprints for Verifying AI Model Decision Behaviour at Run Time, Relevant to Google, NVIDIA and Apple AI Trust Roadmaps
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: This document gives a technical and functional description of Algorithmic Logic Fingerprints (ALF): a way to verify that an AI model or algorithm in production still makes the decisions that were reviewed and approved, and to stop its output from taking effect if it does not. The problem. Current AI trust mechanisms prove identity and origin, not behaviour: Model signing (OpenSSF Model Signing, led by Google, NVIDIA and HiddenLayer; NVIDIA NGC signed models) proves which file a model is. Attestation and transparency logs (for example Apple Private Cloud Compute) prove which software a server runs. Neither shows what the model actually decides. A model can be fine-tuned, quantised, wrapped in a prompt or proxy layer, or replaced behind the same name or signature, and an AI agent can act on its output before anyone notices. How it works. Fingerprint generation. A compact cryptographic fingerprint of decision behaviour is created without access to source code, model weights or training data. For machine-learning models it is built by sampling decision boundaries. For rule-based or traditional code it is built from normalised control-flow and decision structure. Sealed-probe verification. In the highest-assurance mode, the model is tested with a sealed set of inputs that the computing system cannot see in advance. Four views must match together: decision boundaries, monotonicity and consistency, constraint activation, and constraint topology. A different model wrapped to imitate the approved one cannot pass all four. Approved-fingerprint registry. Each approved model or algorithm version has a reference fingerprint that can be checked at any time. Run-time check at the point of effect. Inside a trusted execution environment (for example a confidential VM or a confidential GPU), the live fingerprint is compared with the approved one after computation finishes and before the output is used. Fail-closed enforcement. If the fingerprint does not match, approval is automatically invalidated and the output is withheld. The capability needed to act (send, pay, move, transmit) is not released. Validation receipts. Each decision produces a tamper-evident receipt anchored in a ledger, for audit and incident analysis. Where it applies. The same mechanism applies to AI agents and model-serving platforms, payment and digital-currency systems (including offline wallets), vehicles and robots, and satellites. It complements existing technology rather than replacing it: model signing and model registries (NVIDIA NGC, Google Kaggle); verifiable and confidential AI clouds (Apple Private Cloud Compute, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, AWS, and NVIDIA, Intel and AMD confidential hardware); agent platforms (Google, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services); payment flows (Visa, Mastercard, PayPal, Ant Group); vehicle software governance under UN Regulation 156; Chinese AI platforms (Alibaba, Baidu, ByteDance, Tencent, Huawei, Zhipu AI). It also gives a technical signal for the EU AI Act's substantial-modification rule and for China's generative AI filing regime, both of which depend on knowing whether the deployed system is the one that was assessed. Agentic Commerce and the Economics of Machine-to-Machine Payments
items.abstract: We define agentic commerce as the delegation of commercial decisions and payments to artificial intelligence (AI) and provide statistics on prices and services using data from Coinbase’s x402 Protocol and Tempo & Stripe’s Machine Payments Protocol. Despite more than 234 million recorded transactions, activity across these protocols consists largely of pay-per-use micropayments for digital resources, while observed x402 usage is concentrated among a small number of services, many of which report few paying accounts. Agentic commerce can reduce search and transaction costs, but it also creates governance and accountability problems when AI agents make persistent errors, interact strategically, or are manipulated, potentially generating negative distributional and welfare effects. This review also discusses regulatory approaches and identifies priorities for AI governance and future research.

items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: AI shopping agents discover products, assemble carts, accept terms, pay and track delivery across marketplaces, merchants, payment providers and carriers. Each step produces a signal that is easy to over-read: a recommendation is not consent, a consent screen may not show the shipping charge or the renewal hidden in a free trial, a valid payment credential is not authority for this product and this seller, a marketplace listing may route money to a different beneficiary, a captured charge is not an accepted order, an accepted order is not the right item delivered, and a timeout followed by a retry can charge twice. This disclosure describes a vendor-neutral, non-actuating method for checking that an autonomous purchase stays consistent from intent to outcome. Mandatory requirements are separated from preferences; product, variant, quantity, actual seller, merchant of record and payment beneficiary are bound to the approval; the complete obligation is recomputed in integer minor currency units (unit price × quantity + tax + shipping + fees − discounts) and compared with the checkout total, the approvedmaximum and the remaining shared budget. Admission requires the exact pending operation to match the approved checkout revision under current, unrevoked and unused authority; recurring and trial terms need their own authority; an unknown remote disposition blocks retry until non-acceptance is proven. Payment, order, fulfillment and refund outcomes are kept as separate evidence, and three verdicts — preflight, outcome and overall — are computed in three-valued logic so that a contradiction prevails over unknowns and an unknown outcome is never reported as success. The document provides a 60-stage, six-phase commerce workflow and a separate 52-stage payment-specific workflow, each with flowcharts, 72 plus 64 technical invariants, twelve technical variations, 60 engineering checkpoints, a comparison with existing approaches (agentic checkout protocols, network and wallet tokens, 3-D Secure and strong customer authentication, payment idempotency keys, authorization/capture separation, spending controls, marketplace and payee verification, and subscription regulation) and a non-actuating reference evaluator in Python, JavaScript and Go with 89 shared synthetic vectors, all passing. It never orders, pays or handles credentials; the laboratory is synthetic, self-authored and not peer reviewed. The author is open to acquihire or strategic collaboration. Orchestrating the actions of widely distributed actors and systems has proven difficult. Stablecoin Integration and Stress Transmission Through Crypto-Asset Service Providers: Evidence from Austria
items.abstract: Stablecoins are increasingly entangled with traditional finance, making their response to stress a financial stability concern. However, blockchain pseudonymity and the lack of geographic identifiers force existing work to rely on indirect proxies to infer and locate market participants. In this paper, we exploit a regulatory registry that directly identifies the on-chain addresses of every crypto-asset service provider (CASP) registered in Austria at the end of 2024, reconstructing their Bitcoin, Ether, USDT, and USDC activity through May 2025. Austrian CASPs intermediate roughly $30 billion in cumulative external transfers, while transfers among them are negligible. Combining two transaction-level signals, interaction with CASP cold wallets and on-chain transaction frequency, we classify CASP counterparty activity as retail-like or institutionally mediated. Around stress events, the two groups exhibit distinct flow responses that are obscured in aggregate data. After the FTX bankruptcy, we observe retail-like withdrawals and institutional deposits across assets. After Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) failure, retail-like USDC deposits and institutionally mediated withdrawals are consistent with USDC’s asymmetric redemption access. Registry-based, transaction-level measurements thus offer a reproducible basis for cross-jurisdictional monitoring of how cryptoasset markets transmit risk.

items.title: POLICY-BASED RUNTIME ENFORCEMENT FOR AI AGENTS IN E-COMMERCE: A FRAMEWORK AND EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
items.venue: World Journal of Advanced Engineering Technology and Sciences
items.abstract: E-commerce organizations increasingly give AI agents authority to issue refunds, configure promotions, and handle customer data through tool interfaces such as the Model Context Protocol. Large language models are probabilistic and vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, so model-level guardrails cannot guarantee that agent actions stay within business and regulatory limits. This paper proposes ACE (Agentic Commerce Enforcement), a framework that places a deterministic, policy-driven enforcement layer between agents and commerce systems through four functions: Discover, Observe, Enforce, and Audit. We present a threat model for agentic commerce, a taxonomy of enforceable commerce policies, and a reference architecture. We then evaluate ACE in a controlled experiment of 816 agent runs across two model families (claude-sonnet-4-5 and gpt-6.1-terra) on injection attacks, policy-violating staff requests, and benign tasks. Without enforcement, agents executed harmful actions in 15–43% of attack runs and 67–83% of policy-violating requests. With ACE, harmful execution fell to 0% for both models, with no benign tasks blocked and negligible overhead (≤0.003 ms per task). Which attacks succeeded differed sharply between models, which suggests that commerce security should rest on policy enforcement outside the model rather than on model behavior.

A transaction control layer for governed agentic commerce: reference architecture implementation and controlled evaluation
items.venue: Journal of Computer Science and Technology Studies
items.abstract: A weak answer from a shopping assistant may inconvenience a customer. A weak action from a commerce agent can move money, reserve inventory, change a delivery commitment, or issue a refund. Once an agent can create those effects, the central question is no longer whether its response sounds correct. The question is whether the action is still authorized and commercially valid when the enterprise system commits it. This study introduces a Transaction Control Layer (TCL) that separates an agent's proposal from permission to execute. TCL binds each approved action to grounded intent, delegated authority, current authoritative state, a short validity period, and a stable idempotency key. It then records and reconciles the resulting side effects. We formalize commit validity across five dimensions and define five operational decisions: allow, modify, hold, deny, and escalate. The design is examined with CAV-Bench v1.0.0, an Apache-2.0 reference artifact containing 40 synthetic scenarios and five deterministic architecture profiles. The direct profile reaches an outcome success rate of 0.925, yet only 0.250 of its runs are commit-valid. Adding policy checks, commit-time guards, reconciliation, and lifecycle recovery raises commit-valid success to 0.500, 0.750, 0.875, and 1.000. These values show that the benchmark responds to the controls it was designed to test. They do not estimate real model failure rates or establish production effectiveness. An external replication protocol is therefore included as the next step toward independent validation.

items.title: Agents That Pay: Why a Count of Refusals Is Not Enough, and What a Series for Each Agent Adds
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: AI agents can now pay on a person's behalf. Pine Labs (P3P on UPI), NPCI, Razorpay, Visa, Mastercard, Google (AP2), OpenAI with Stripe (ACP) and the agent-card providers each fix an agent's limits before it starts, and each refuses a request outside them. This note points to one gap that is the same in all of them. A refusal is counted or dropped, but the pattern of refusals over time is not read. Two agents can show the same count of refusals while only one is losing control. The remedy is one refusals series for each agent, with a lag-1 warning number calculated from it. The number rises during a run of refusals, before any cap is reached. A computer-decided shunting action then moves that agent's doubtful payments aside for checking, while every other agent and payment carries on. The note tabulates how each system limits an agent today, shows where the series attaches in each one, and compares the method with the closest published work. Keywords: agentic payments, AI agents, UPI, P3P, AP2, lag-1 autocorrelation, early warning, shunting action, Intent List

items.title: From Intent to Effect: 639 Proposed Direction for AI Safety and 48-Stage Workflows for Three-Valued Operational Consistency in AI-Driven Infrastructure
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.abstract: Autonomous and AI-driven systems now issue operations whose consequences land far from where they were decided: in radio-access-network controllers, operator charging systems, device queues and DMA engines, robot actuators, emergency broadcast channels, payment rails, browsers, and long-running agent processes that migrate between hosts. Across all of these, a recurring failure appears. A system treats an acknowledgement, a status code, a callback, a log entry, or its own internal view as if it were proof that the intended effect occurred, on the intended target, under the conditions that were authorized. Observations are fused across mismatched clocks, identities, and configuration generations; agreements are treated as execution authority; partial effects are retried as if nothing happened; translated or transformed instructions are delivered as though they preserved their original meaning. This disclosure addresses that gap as a single architectural problem expressed across many domains. The disclosure presents a 280-page technical record comprising common-workflow flowcharts, phase-level engineering figures, implementation flowcharts, and 639 proposed patent claims. Its unifying principle is that the original authorized operation retains a stable identity from which every downstream representation, transformation, dispatch, acknowledgement, and observed effect must be separately reconstructed and qualified. Each workflow applies a conservative three-valued rule at every gate: all mandatory predicates supported advances; any predicate contradicted inhibits or raises an exception; any predicate unresolved holds. Final outcomes are expressed as scoped verdicts (CONSISTENT, INCONSISTENT, or UNRESOLVED) with the evidence, resource state, and gaps on which each verdict depends. Throughout, acknowledgement is distinguished from effect, observation from authority, eligibility from authorization, and historical records from current permission. The record is organized into technical groups, each with its own common workflow and claim set: Group A (claims 1–40) governs observation-to-control consistency in radio-access-network calculations: reconstructing resource identity and configuration generation, bounding temporal applicability under clock uncertainty, preserving measurement semantics across interfaces, selecting dependency-aware joint observations, maintaining consistency through controller migration and failover, and revalidating material dependencies before a control result is delivered. Group B (claims 41–80) addresses multi-agent network incident diagnosis and repair, covering source-qualified evidence provenance and independence, competing fault hypotheses resolved by discriminating evidence, repair-plan applicability under concurrent changes, asynchronous repair with partial-effect reconstruction, independent post-repair verification of recovery and adverse effects, and distributed incident history with recurrence analysis. Group C (claims 81–120) maintains telecommunications session lifecycle consistency across subscriber trust changes (SIM/eSIM), home and visited operator roaming and partial release, concurrent programmable quality-on-demand operations, user-plane usage, quota and charging lineage, purpose-scoped consent versus actual network effect, and partial operator outage with deferred settlement. Group D (claims 121–160) reconstructs hardware observation-to-effect consistency through independent hardware observers, CPU-to-device DMA memory continuity, device queue and descriptor occupancy, firmware and configuration invalidation, and cross-stage representation of external effects. Group E (claims 161–200) holds that negotiated agreement is not execution authority among multiple agents, covering versioned negotiation and partial acceptance, streaming artifacts and delegated sub-actions, amendment impact across versions, cancellation and late effects, partitioned participant views, and residual obligations at closure. Group F (claims 201–240) treats asynchronous tool and protocol operations, including durable task identity and callback origin, tool-schema generation and in-flight semantic change, acknowledged subscription and push-event coverage, resource alias and generation continuity, cancellation and retry with residual external effects, and concurrent usage-budget settlement. Group G (claims 241–280) translates machine-readable robot skills into calibration-qualified physical capability, evaluated by an independent safety controller, admitted under time-bounded command contracts, downgraded at runtime when capability degrades mid-actuation, transferred between robots without reusing unverified calibration, and closed by independent physical-effect observation. Group H (claims 281–320) carries emergency instructions from source to physical response: original instruction identity and provenance, extraction and preservation of safety-critical meaning, multilingual translation verification under uncertainty, recipient-specific exact-content dispatch, correction and supersession, and readback and response verification. Group M1 (claims 321–380) governs autonomous AI commerce from original purchase intent to actual commercial outcome, covering product, variant and seller continuity, complete monetary exposure at dynamic checkout, current purchasing authority, payment-mandate-to-financial-effect consistency, multi-agent shared budgets, and post-purchase fulfilment, refund, and correction. Group M2 (claims 381–440) operates at silicon level, binding an authorized operation to the hardware command a device actually consumes, through descriptor integrity, effective DMA translation and invalidation, reset and assignment incarnation, protected command admission with atomic use-state, shared quota admission, and cross-path effectuation coverage. Claims 441–509 extend the architecture to protected virtual-machine and sandbox runtimes with consequence-bound egress, dual-boundary digital-to-physical command enforcement, controller-local authority without transferable tokens, protected credential release, buffered physical-command invalidation, crash-resistant authority recovery, authority preservation across checkpoint, fork, migration and changing delegation, and separation of informative context from consequential execution. Group I (claims 510–539, with 600–639) secures browser and graphical-agent actions by binding an authorized task to the actual interface target, frame, origin, redirect, and background request it produces, and extends this to interface-independent control across graphical, voice, remote, native, and terminal interfaces. Group J (claims 540–599, with 600–639) preserves a persistent agent task’s logical identity, authority, outstanding external exposure, and callbacks across migration between execution instances, using generation fencing, representation-independent current authority, and callback-independent outcome verification, including treatment of partial and streaming effects without duplicate repetition. The material is offered as a public technical disclosure and reference architecture. The claims are proposed, not granted, and the figures describe implementation designs rather than guarantees of novelty, freedom to operate, or regulatory compliance. Safety-related content, including robotic and emergency-communication workflows, is non-certified and makes no SIL, PL, or standards-conformance claim. The record is intended for system architects, network and hardware engineers, AI-agent developers, standards contributors, and regulators concerned with accountable autonomy, where the question is not only whether an action was permitted, but whether what actually happened corresponds to what was authorized. items.title: AI shopping agents and the reallocation of consumer attention: seller visibility and platform access in agentic commerce
items.venue: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
items.abstract: Purpose This study develops a theoretical model of how AI shopping agents reallocate shopping activity, reshape seller visibility and alter platform control in digital commerce. Consumer attention is defined as the allocation of shopping episodes across channels, distinct from visual or cognitive attention. Design/methodology/approach A two-seller platform model compares platform-mediated and AI-agent-mediated shopping. The platform chooses agent access and ranking bias; sellers choose price, platform-facing visibility and agent-facing adaptation. Heterogeneous AI-use costs make channel use endogenous, while a fixed implementation cost creates an adaptation threshold. Extensions separate information access from transaction execution and test the robustness of the analytical regimes numerically. Findings Agent access is profitable when transaction and AI-channel gains outweigh lost ranking monetization and governance costs, and information access may remain open while transaction execution is restricted. Sellers activate agent-facing adaptation only when its incremental return covers implementation cost. AI-mediated shopping lowers prices when comparison pressure dominates verified differentiation. Ranking mismatch can turn the two visibility investments from complements into competing activities, and privately optimal openness can fall outside the welfare-improving interval. Originality/value Four features distinguish AI shopping agents from platform recommenders and comparison sites: delegated choice authority, cross-platform scope, multi-stage task execution and an independently governed ranking layer. The framework links these features to layered platform access, endogenous AI-channel use, distinct visibility investments, implementation costs, verifiable trust signals and divergence between private and social incentives in agentic commerce.

Enterprise Agent Identity Governance Framework (EAIGF): A Policy-Mediated Identity and Access Governance Model for Autonomous Digital Workforce Systems
items.venue: International Journal of Cyber Threat Intelligence and Secure Networking
items.abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are evolving from passive decision-support tools into autonomous digital workers capable of planning, reasoning, invoking tools, accessing enterprise resources, and executing business actions with varying degrees of autonomy. While enterprises maintain mature governance models for human identities, service accounts, and application identities, existing Identity and Access Management (IAM) frameworks do not adequately address the governance challenges introduced by autonomous agents. Unlike conventional applications, agents dynamically determine execution paths, invoke reusable skills, delegate tasks to peer agents, and perform privileged actions across enterprise systems. These characteristics define a new class of enterprise identity that requires dedicated governance, authorization, and accountability controls. This paper proposes the Enterprise Agent Identity Governance Framework (EAIGF), which treats autonomous agents as first-class enterprise identities subject to lifecycle management, quantitative trust classification, privileged access governance, and end-to-end accountability. The framework's principal constructs form an identity layer comprising the Agent Identity Registry (AIR), the Agent Provisioning Certificate, Agent Trust Tiering driven by an explicit Agent Identity Risk Score (AIRS) formula, Agent Privileged Access Management (Agent-PAM), and a Delegated Trust Chain with Agent Identity Lineage for multi-agent accountability. These constructs are enforced through a policy-mediated runtime boundary that performs capability projection and risk-adaptive authorization. A reference implementation realizing the registry, the AIRS formula, capability projection, and risk-adaptive authorization correctly enforced all ten governance scenarios in the evaluation with zero false-permits on disallowed capabilities and a mean authorization overhead of approximately 0.015 ms per request. A larger randomized evaluation over 600 authorization requests across 80 agents and 25 reusable skills reproduced this result and, against a naive whole-skill authorization baseline, reduced the exposed capability surface by 66.7 percent while blocking every attempted privilege escalation through delegation. A synthetic financial-services walkthrough demonstrates how Identity Governance and Administration (IGA), Privileged Access Management (PAM), and Zero Trust principles extend to agentic environments. EAIGF provides a practical blueprint for governing autonomous agents at scale while preserving least privilege, accountability, and operational resilience.

items.title: Resource Locks and Fast Unlock for Shared Balances in Certificate-Based Payment Systems
items.abstract: Certificate-based payment systems such as FastPay settle a payment with one round of signatures from a quorum of validators and avoid global ordering. The client collects the signatures, and validators never talk to each other. We observe that this client-driven design is complete only as long as no lock is ever undone. Each account has a single writer, a conflict can only come from that writer's own misbehavior, and the account stays locked as the penalty. Stablecoin payments routinely need balances that several accounts debit: treasuries, merchant pools, allowances and subscriptions. There, honest accounts race, locks must be undone, and a quorum certificate held privately by a client can be silently overridden. We prove that no unlock rule is safe in this setting unless certificate formation is visible to validators. We present a hybrid protocol. Personal accounts keep the client-driven FastPay path unchanged. A shared resource is a balance with its own version number and a set of authorized accounts. Transactions on shared resources are submitted to any validator and certified by a two-phase broadcast, ECHO then READY. The admission check requires both the sender's nonce and the resource's nonce to be free. Without contention, this path needs no consensus. When concurrent debits split the votes in any proportion, validators detect the split themselves, freeze the affected resource version, and resolve it with one agreement instance scoped to that version. Losing transactions return their sender nonce. We prove consistency, no overdraft, validity, finality and liveness. The protocol composes with the PDCC reconfiguration protocol.

items.title: Developing Consumer Trust in Sustainable Agentic Commerce: Conditional Signals, Auditable Governance, and Justified Non-Purchase Advice
items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) changes digital retail from consumer-led search to delegated decision making, increasing both the potential value and the agency risks of recommendation. This conceptual article asks the following: Under what architectural and governance conditions can an autonomous shopping agent earn calibrated consumer trust while supporting economically and environmentally appropriate consumption decisions? Using a purposive, multidisciplinary synthesis of signaling theory, principal–agent theory, the ability–benevolence–integrity model of trust, trustworthy AI, recommender system governance, and sustainable consumption research, we develop a process model linking four architectural features to consumer perceptions, delegation, reliance, and decision outcomes. The features are scoped provenance verification, disclosed and audited commercial incentives, faithful contrastive explanations, and active evaluation of retention, repair, refurbishment, and purchase. We argue that justified non-purchase advice can function as a credible signal of consumer alignment only when the operator is the signal sender, the advice creates observable opportunity or accountability costs, and compensation and audit arrangements make imitation more costly for a misaligned operator. The framework distinguishes perceived trustworthiness from overall trust, willingness to delegate, actual reliance, recommendation appropriateness, and lifecycle sustainability. A five-layer architecture, a worked decision example, and four testable propositions specify how missing data, conflicting preferences, uncertainty, authorization, privacy, and accountability should be handled. This article treats the applications as illustrations rather than empirical cases and concludes with limitations and an empirical research agenda focused on calibrated—not merely increased—trust.

I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
items.abstract: Human oversight is a pillar of AI safety. It is often exercised by a human in the loop (HITL) who approves critical actions taken by an AI agent. AI agents' increasing ability to bypass guardrails, though, raises the question of how to enforce HITL robustly. We introduce the concept of inalienable human-in-the-loop (I-HITL). An I-HITL protocol ensures that an agent can initiate an action only with explicit human approval, even when the human interacts with a system (e.g., a local agentic harness) compromised by the agent. A strong I-HITL protocol additionally ensures such approval even when an adversarial human attempts to delegate approvals to an agent. To motivate I-HITL, we report on experiments with a popular agentic wallet platform in which raising an agent's spending cap requires HITL approval via emailed one-time passcodes (OTPs). Given access to the user's email and a task blocked by the cap, we find that ten different frontier models will often autonomously raise the cap, harvesting OTPs to bypass a HITL guardrail and surfacing other vulnerabilities. We formally define I-HITL using the concept of communication topologies and prove necessary and sufficient conditions for its realization. We show that an I-HITL protocol requires a trusted entity - a trusted computing device (or equivalent) - and characterize which such devices can and cannot realize an I-HITL protocol. We present a prototype I-HITL system called Countersign that can plug into and strengthen existing HITL systems using off-the-shelf consumer mobile devices.

items.title: Breaking the Peg, or Not: The Limited Power of Oracle Manipulation Against Early Stablecoin Depeg Prediction
items.abstract: A common worry about depeg predictors is that an adversary who manipulates oracle prices can blind them. We test it on a new multi-source corpus of twelve historical stress episodes across nine assets and three chains. Under retrospective leave-one-event-out testing, the reconstructed models span 0.558–0.772 ROC-AUC, with our reference predictor at 0.762; the source papers report different metrics and tasks that are not directly comparable. Manipulable price features hurt out-of-event generalization: on the seven-episode live-feed subgroup, retained features reach 0.75 AUC versus 0.72 for the full model, directional, not significant at seven events. We define the Oracle Manipulation Index (OMI), prove that shifting the aggregate by δ while one honest feed survives forces the unnormalized cross-feed price range to be at least δ/L for L-Lipschitz aggregators, and measure on a Foundry mainnet fork (Curve 3pool, block 25,238,878) that a 0.1% move requires about USD 50 M in deployed capital. Excluding individually affordable channels gives a sufficient input-invariance rule under fixed channel costs; the robust subset matches clean accuracy and degrades less under tested synthetic attacks in point estimate (directional, not significant at seven events). OMI’s empirical lift is modest and regime-dependent (pooled 0.0037, not significant; it helps off-chain and multi-venue settings, not single-venue on-chain ones), and precision is low (about 33 false-positive windows per true-positive window at 10% recall). Within this early-warning setting, oracle manipulation is a weak evasion vector because the tested subset is empirically less sensitive to the evaluated perturbations.

items.title: FlockWorld: Toward Population-Scale Multi-Agent Video World Models through Artificial Life Simulation
items.abstract: Most action-conditioned video world models remain limited to a single player, while existing multiplayer models support only small, fixed groups of agents. We introduce FlockWorld, an artificial-life environment built on Reynolds's Boids algorithm for studying population-scale multi-agent video world models. Specifically, FlockWorld renders synchronized egocentric crops, assigns distinct colors to preserve camera-agent identity across views, exposes rule-derived accelerations as actions, and lets the number of camera agents be configured independently of the size of the surrounding population. We further introduce FlockDiT, an action-conditioned latent diffusion transformer trained with flow matching on FlockWorld data to jointly generate synchronized egocentric videos for multiple agents. Our results suggest that joint generation benefits agent detection at density-matched settings and that diffusion forcing improves rollout fidelity. Together, FlockWorld and FlockDiT provide a controlled testbed for multi-agent video generation.

Markets of Minds: A 51-Billion-State Economy of Intelligence
items.abstract: When intelligence is shared, reasoning becomes a constrained allocation problem. In a population of agents with limited access to expert models, an intervention can benefit its recipient yet still be a poor use of shared capacity if another feasible intervention has greater expected value. Assistance must therefore be evaluated through both its marginal benefit and the opportunity cost induced by budgets, access, scarcity, and service capacity. To this end, we introduce Markets of Minds, a framework for allocating expert reasoning across agents before expert outputs are observed. For each feasible agent-service pair, the framework estimates the expected gain from assistance relative to the agent's default continuation, explicitly separating repair benefit from regression risk, and jointly clears assistance contracts under shared resource constraints. We then study this problem in a dependency-aware agent economy with 51.2 billion addressable persona-market states spanning capabilities, cognitive budgets, provider access, scarcity, and network roles. These dependencies couple allocation feasibility across agents rather than the outcome of a fixed contract. Empirically, in a matched replay of 240 cases under a common 30% assistance quota, the frozen allocator reaches 85.42% task-level persona adherence versus 73.86% for equal-capacity random allocation, a gain of 11.56 percentage points. The results show that assistance value is heterogeneous and can be negative, and that scarcity changes which interventions are worth purchasing. Together, these findings motivate a population-level view of intelligence where the value of assistance depends not only on what it can achieve, but also on which alternative uses of scarce cognitive capacity it displaces.

Price insurance or cash-flow insurance? Energy subsidies and targeted transfers in a heterogeneous-agent economy
items.abstract: This paper examines whether generalized energy subsidies or targeted cash transfers provide more effective stabilization in an economy with heterogeneous households and segmented labor markets. We develop a small-open-economy Heterogeneous-Agent New Keynesian (HANK-DSGE) model calibrated to Morocco, incorporating heterogeneity in marginal propensities to consume (MPCs), formal–informal–agricultural labor-market segmentation, imported energy, remittances, and exchange-rate management. An agricultural productivity experiment identifies sectoral wage adjustment as an important mechanism transmitting shocks through household labor income. The central policy experiment compares generalized energy subsidies with subsidy removal and a budget-neutral reallocation of the same state-contingent fiscal outlay toward targeted transfers. Targeted transfers direct 81.8% of expenditure toward high-MPC households, compared with 10.6% of the dividend-mediated incidence of subsidies. Following an oil-price shock, redirecting subsidy expenditure toward targeted transfers reduces the impact consumption loss from 1.05% to 0.51% and the welfare loss from 0.40% to 0.22%, while increasing short-run inflation pass-through. The results identify a policy frontier between price insurance and cash-flow insurance and show that MPC-weighted fiscal incidence is central to the stabilization effects of alternative fiscal instruments. items.title: SaaS in the Agent Economy: Why AI Just Changed Bootstrapped SaaS Forever [video]
Proof-Carrying Contracts: Commitments AI Agents Cannot Break
items.abstract: AI agents increasingly act on behalf of people or other agents, purchasing services, exchanging information and delegating work. What an agent must respect is written in instructions, policies or agreements, but text alone cannot make it comply. It may make mistakes, be redirected by what it reads, or pursue different interests. For an economy of such agents to function, parties need agreements they can rely on without inspecting or trusting one another's agents. We introduce Proof-Carrying Contracts (PC2), a framework for making agreed constraints enforceable throughout an agent's interactions with a system. Before a requested operation can run, the agent must supply a machine-checkable proof that it preserves the agreed constraints in every case allowed by its model. An execution system called the Airlock checks the proof and controls access to the operation. The parties specify the conditions to preserve, while the agent supplies the reasoning needed to justify its decisions and remains free to adapt its strategy. This avoids having to design a separate permission policy and prove that every decision it permits is safe. We prove that the constraints hold at every instant during execution, even for an adversarial agent, and identify when this implies safety in the world. Reusable capability modules provide tools and guarantees from which contracts can be constructed. PC2 provides a foundation for an agent economy whose agreements protect both those delegating work and those carrying it out.

items.title: Banking hours and stablecoin peg repair: evidence from the SVB-USDC episode
Provable Authority: A Protocol for Verifiable Authority Resolution and Control Across Human, Organizational, and Agentic Transactions
items.abstract: Payment systems authenticate users, devices, accounts, and cryptographic credentials, but a relying party, such as a counterparty, payment rail, marketplace, or autonomous agent runtime, generally cannot obtain compact, independently verifiable evidence that the party presenting one exact transaction holds current organizational authority to execute it under the applicable evidence, policy, budget, and approval state. Agentic commerce makes this gap operationally urgent: a software agent can produce a valid signature while acting outside its delegated purpose, after its sponsor's authority has changed, or on transaction details that differ from those a human approved. We describe the ChainIT Authority Protocol, a subject-neutral and rail-neutral pre-execution authority and evidence control plane. The protocol separates durable identity, a versioned organizational authority record (the Authority Resolution Pactvera), sourced evidence assertions, deterministic reason-coded policy predicates, and organization-configured dispositions; binds each decision and human approval to a canonical transaction digest; reserves capacity atomically so that limits hold under concurrency; and authorizes commit only through a single-use, sender-constrained Execution Authorization Credential consumed at the rail adapter, with append-only lifecycle evidence sealed after the terminal outcome. An Agent Subject Profile adds the workload registration, attested key hierarchy, and sovereignty boundary required when the acting subject is an AI agent, without introducing a separate authority concept. We specify the commit-time execution predicate and bounded-freshness status rules, give enforcement profiles for fiat (ACH, wire, card, instant payment) and stablecoin rails, and state residual risks and non-goals.

items.title: From authorization to defensibility: enterprise stablecoin compliance readiness after the GENIUS Act
items.venue: Journal of Financial Regulation and Compliance
items.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how organizational actors translate statutory authorization of payment stablecoins into judgments of compliance readiness for enterprise use. Design/methodology/approach The study uses 23 short stimulus-based interviews conducted after the U.S. GENIUS Act: 22 organizational informants and one finance-domain informant. Abductive thematic analysis combined evidence weighting, negative cases and stimulus and timing sensitivity checks. Findings Authorization increased discussability but not defensibility. Readiness required workflow value, an assurance bundle, operational absorbability, gatekeeper movement and a credible regulatory signal. Some participants instead regarded stablecoins as redundant because existing rails already met their needs; where value existed, unresolved custody, controls, systems and counterparty acceptance delayed use. Research limitations/implications The data capture first-pass, role-informed judgments in a short, network-recruited design; they do not observe deliberation or implementation. The construct is a sensitizing framework, not a tested causal model. Practical implications The framework provides a diagnostic: identify the payment pain, document assurance, test operational fit and locate the blocking gatekeeper. Social implications Public-payer, healthcare and nonprofit cases show that modernization can affect access, confidentiality, stewardship and familiar payment options. Originality/value The paper develops regulatory-compliance readiness lag: the perceived interval between legal authorization and organizationally defensible payment use.

items.title: Cryptographically Secure Agent-to-Agent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) comprise AI agents that collaborate or compete to perform complex, distributed tasks. Their dynamic interactions create opportunities for threat actors to target and impersonate other agents, intercept messages, inject malicious prompts, and exfiltrate sensitive data while simultaneously complicating the detection of anomalous behavior through conventional monitoring. This paper surveys threats and cryptographic challenges in agent-to-agent communication and presents a zero-trust architecture integrating identity, transport security, message integrity, and monitoring. The architecture establishes agent identities via decentralized identifiers and task-scoped verifiable credentials backed by a permissioned ledger, enforcing least-privilege authorization. For transport security, it provides mutually authenticated, crypto-agile TLS with hybrid post-quantum key establishment, and evaluates KEMTLS with pre-distributed public keys to reduce handshake overhead. Signed CBOR envelopes preserve payload integrity across multi-hop exchanges, while zero-knowledge proofs verify declared task constraints without exposing underlying inputs. Context-aware monitoring of inter-agent messages, tool activity, and execution telemetry informs the setting of risk-based trust thresholds and supports the detection of behavioral anomalies. Together, these mechanisms provide an integrated framework for securing and auditing agent communication, with implications for other agentic protocols and prospective 6G semantic communication.

items.title: Approve What, Exactly? Effect Binding and Trusted Rendering for Agent Step-Up Authorization
items.abstract: AI agents now pause for approval before they send money, delete files or email outsiders, and that approval is usually treated as a second factor. We argue it is one only when compromising the agent cannot produce it and when it names exactly what it approves, and we test both conditions. We define twelve attacks on the approval path, including decoy recipients, amount cancellation, card padding, label spoofing, enrollment squatting and threshold splitting, and run them against the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), the Microsoft action-bound approval design and Model Context Protocol (MCP) elicitation. An audit of ten agent runtimes finds no third-party verifiable approval record, no flood limits where measurable, and post-approval argument changes in four of eight runtimes with measurable binding. As a reference defense we build ASU (Agent Step-Up), a gateway that renders the approval card from a canonical effect descriptor, has a passkey on the phone of the user sign its digest, and executes only the stored call. Tamarin proves its binding, single-use and key-level non-repudiation properties under three stated hypotheses (53 lemmas). Across 27,108 scripted trials and 609 AgentDojo attack pairs, ASU stops substitution, replay and grant stretching, and the trusted card cuts forged-narration attack success from 0.54 to 0.03. With 15 current language models as automated approvers, the trusted card raises the attack catch rate from 0.30 to 0.98, at the cost of refusing 16 percent of harmless near misses, mostly due to a placeholder artifact in our stimuli. A second device adds nothing measurable over a trusted on-host confirmation in these experiments, flooding still succeeds 0.45 to 0.60 of the time against a modeled approver, and approval cannot stop effects that policy already allows. Code, data and proofs: https://github.com/Sports-Vision-Inc/agent-step-up

items.title: Chính sách quản lý Agent Economy trong thời đại số: bài học kinh nghiệm cho việt nam Policy Frameworks for Governing the Agent Economy in the Digital Age: Lessons for Vietnam
items.venue: Tạp chí Khoa học và Công nghệ Trường Đại học Công nghệ Đông Á
items.abstract: The rapid emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is ushering in a new “Agent Economy” (AE), in which autonomous AI agents act on behalf of humans to perform complex tasks. While the Agent Economy promises substantial gains in productivity and innovation, it simultaneously presents profound governance challenges related to data privacy, security, ethics, and job displacement. A pressing concern is how humans can effectively oversee and regulate an AI-driven economy that may expand beyond the reach of traditional governance mechanisms. This study adopts a literature synthesis and comparative policy analysis approach to propose a six-pillar policy framework tailored for Vietnam. The framework aims to simultaneously foster AI development and mitigate associated risks in the digital age, thereby laying a strategic foundation for Vietnam to engage proactively, safely, and effectively with the Agent Economy.

items.title: Nonlinear Identification and Early Warning of Stablecoin Price Depegging: Empirical Evidence Based on a Cusp Catastrophe Model
items.abstract: Stablecoin prices stay close to $1 most of the time, but in a few periods they deviate markedly. Using daily data on four stablecoins (USDT, USDC, DAI, and FRAX) from 2019 to 2023, we introduce a cusp catastrophe model to identify the depegging process and compare two measures, price deviation and log return. We find the following. First, the jumps identified under the two measures differ substantially: jumps are sparse under the price deviation measure and frequent under the log return measure. Price deviation corresponds to the degree of departure from the peg, whereas log return corresponds to short-term price movements, so an assessment of stablecoin stability should distinguish these two dimensions. Second, differences in jump behavior depend on market embeddedness and the supply-and-demand adjustment mechanism. Traditional financial market variables are most broadly associated with price deviations of USDT and USDC. Although both are fiat-backed, the expansion of market capitalization works in opposite directions for USDT and USDC. For USDT it is associated with larger deviations because of issuance and distribution frictions, whereas for USDC it is associated with converging deviations through a direct redemption channel. Hence, the level of risk depends on liquidity characteristics and redemption arrangements. Third, on-chain capital flows and holdings concentration have forward-looking early-warning power for depegging; moderate deviations are best monitored over short horizons, and severe depegging is identified most effectively over a 7-day horizon. We provide empirical evidence from a nonlinear perspective for understanding the micro-level pricing mechanism of digital assets.

items.title: Get In, Decide, Prove: A Merchant-Side Readiness Benchmark for Agentic Commerce
items.abstract: AI agents now browse and buy on people's behalf, and benchmarks measure how well the agents perform. Far less is known about the other side of the transaction: whether a merchant's website lets an agent in, publishes terms precise enough to decide a purchase, and leaves evidence of what was agreed. This paper presents a merchant-side benchmark built on those three questions and reports a pilot of it. The central measurement, decision sufficiency, rates each criterion of a concrete buyer mandate (total cost, cancellation or return terms, service date, variant identity) as determinate, indeterminate, or unknown from the merchant's own published evidence. Readiness scores carry their evidence coverage and missingness bounds; access is reported separately for a declared bot, a declared headless browser, and a user-present browser; and each observed term is mapped to the RAILS admissibility class of the evidence that could support it in a dispute. Four large merchants received the full assessment: three refused the declared profiles at their offer pages, and no mandate could be confirmed as met, because each merchant left a total or a refund term undetermined. An access census of 555 sites of merchants that two payment processors publicly name as clients found the home page unreadable to both declared profiles at 105 sites (18.9%). A declared assessment of 330 merchants, scored by deterministic rules without a rater, found that evidence coverage rather than the score decides who can be ranked: 115 merchants (35%) reached the ranking threshold, rankable profiles scored a median of 89 to 90, and material terms was the one pillar well below the others, because the all-in total was decidable at 18 merchants. The pilot shows that the measurements can be taken; it does not validate them or rank merchants, and the weights and the projected clearing band await validation against outcomes.

items.title: Cryptomercantilism vs Monetary Sovereignty: How Stablecoin Laws Shape the Battle for International Monetary Supremacy
items.abstract: Stablecoins are privately issued cryptocurrencies whose value is pegged to official currencies such as the US dollar. Their ease of use on the global level opens up a new front in global currency competition. This article asks how the EU and US—the issuers of the world’s two leading currencies—approach stablecoins through their respective legal frameworks. We contrast a US strategy of cryptomercantilism with an EU strategy of monetary sovereignty. These strategies yield legal frameworks that look similar on the surface but diverge sharply in substance. The US’s GENIUS Act aims to enhance the dollar’s dominance in global payment systems and stimulate new demand for US assets, particularly government bonds. The EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCAR) serves to safeguard the state’s ability to govern money. We conclude by discussing how the euro area and other countries can react to US cryptomercantilism, highlighting new challenges related to regulatory equivalence agreements and fungibility of tokens issued in different jurisdictions.
